blocks.title: In one sentence

paragraphs.t: Every pattern in the catalog, shown in software people know — chosen on one rule, that the company wrote the decision down — with the problem, the pattern, the named cases, and the cost.

blocks.title: In plain words

paragraphs.t: Every pattern in the catalog, told through software people know: Amazon’s product page, Netflix’s move to the cloud, Uber’s 2,200 services, Airbnb’s migration, Shopify’s decision to stay a monolith, Stripe’s idempotency keys, LinkedIn’s Kafka. Each mini-chapter has the same four beats — the problem, the pattern, the named examples, the cost — so the patterns become stories with a bill attached. Under every chapter heading this edition adds one line in plain words.

runs.t: Answer 3 set out the pattern language and Answer 4 listed its catalog. This answer takes each pattern in turn and explains it through software that many people have used or read about: Amazon, Netflix, Uber, Airbnb, Shopify, Stripe, LinkedIn, Twitter, Google, Facebook, Spotify, Monzo, Zalando, Microsoft’s
eShopOnContainers
reference application, and the open-source platforms — Kubernetes,
Kafka
Envoy
, Istio, Prometheus — that grew out of those companies’ needs.
The examples are chosen on one rule: the company or project wrote the decision down, in an engineering blog, a paper, a conference talk, or an open-source repository, so the claim can be checked.

Dates are the year the practice was published, not the year it began. Companies change; each example describes the system as it was described at the time, and several chapters include a case where a company later moved the other way.
Every chapter has the same four parts. The problem: what goes wrong without the pattern. The pattern: what it prescribes, in Richardson’s terms. One or more named examples.
The cost: what the pattern charges, because a pattern with no cost is a slogan.
A source line closes each chapter.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: What is built, shipped, and started as one thing.
A component that spreads incoming requests across identical copies.
One deployable unit whose internal boundaries are enforced in the code.
A complete copy of the application with its own database; a shop lives in exactly one. Not the Kubernetes pod.
How much is affected when one thing fails.

blocks.title: In plain words: One program, one deploy, one database. The simplest thing that can work — and often the right thing.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
One program, one deploy, one database. The simplest thing that can work — and often the right thing.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

A team has to ship a product, and every distributed boundary is a cost before it is a benefit. Network calls, partial failure, and per-service pipelines are paid for on day one; the benefits arrive only when the organization is large enough to need independent releases.
💡 The pattern.
The user interface, the domain logic, and the data access are one deployable unit: one build, one process image, one database.
Scaling is by running more identical copies behind a load balancer. Structure inside the unit is a matter of code organization, not of deployment.
Shopify.

Shopify runs one of the largest Ruby on Rails codebases in existence and has kept it a monolith. In “Deconstructing the Monolith” (2019), Kirsten Westeinde describes the choice not to split into services but to reorganize the code into components with enforced boundaries — the modular monolith — with a tool, later open-sourced as Packwerk (2020), that fails the build when one component reaches into another’s internals. Horizontal scale comes from “pods”: each pod is a complete copy of the application with its own MySQL, and a shop lives in exactly one pod.
Stack Overflow.

Nick Craver’s 2016 architecture write-ups show the Q&A sites served by a single .NET application on nine web servers with a SQL Server pair, handling hundreds of millions of page views a month. Basecamp’s David Heinemeier Hansson argued the same position in “The Majestic Monolith” (2016): for a small team, one well-organized codebase is the faster path.
Amazon Prime Video, Segment.

Two documented returns. In 2023 the Prime Video audio/video quality monitoring team moved a pipeline built from Step Functions, Lambda, and S3 into a single ECS process and reported roughly a 90 percent drop in infrastructure cost, because the orchestration and the object-store traffic between steps dominated the bill. In 2018 Segment consolidated about 140 per-destination services back into one, because shared libraries drifted across the services and testing and deploying them separately had become the work.
⚠️ The cost.
One release train, one runtime, and one blast radius. A bad deploy affects every feature. Internal boundaries hold only as long as the team enforces them, which is why Shopify built a tool to do it.

Source: Westeinde, Shopify Engineering, 2019; Packwerk, 2020. Craver, “Stack Overflow: The Architecture” series, 2016. Hansson, “The Majestic Monolith,” 2016. Kolny, Prime Video Tech, 2023. Noonan, “Goodbye Microservices,” Segment, 2018.

blocks.title: In plain words: Many small programs, each owned by a small team, each with its own data, talking over the network.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Many small programs, each owned by a small team, each with its own data, talking over the network.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
One codebase and one release train stop scaling with the organization. Many teams wait on one deploy. One failure takes the whole product down. One technology has to fit every job.
💡 The pattern.
The application is a set of services, each independently deployable and loosely coupled, each owned by a small team, each with its own data.
Lewis and Fowler’s 2014 article named the characteristics: organized around business capabilities, decentralized data management, smart endpoints and dumb pipes, products not projects.
Amazon.

Around 2002 Jeff Bezos issued the mandate that Steve Yegge later summarized: all teams expose their data and functionality through service interfaces; teams communicate only through those interfaces; no direct database reads, no shared memory; every interface is designed as if it could be exposed to the outside. Werner Vogels described the result in 2006: the team that builds a service runs it, and a single product page draws on more than a hundred services. Amazon Web Services grew out of that service-team culture.
Netflix.

In August 2008 a database corruption stopped DVD shipments for three days. From 2009 Netflix moved its streaming system to AWS and rebuilt its monolithic Java application as hundreds of services. The last data center closed in January 2016. The pieces Netflix built along the way — Eureka, Hystrix, Zuul, Ribbon, Archaius — were released as
Netflix OSS
and became the reference implementations for a generation.
Uber and Monzo.

Uber grew from a Python monolith to about 2,200 critical microservices by 2020, when it had to introduce a domain layer above them. Monzo, a bank founded in 2015, was built on microservices in Go from the start and had about 1,500 services by 2019.
⚠️ The cost.

Distributed-systems problems become everyday problems: partial failure, latency, data consistency across owners, and the operational tooling to see any of it. The remaining chapters of this document are the bill for this decision.

Source: Yegge’s 2011 account of the Bezos mandate. Vogels, “A Conversation with Werner Vogels,” ACM Queue, 2006. Izrailevsky, “Completing the Netflix Cloud Migration,” 2016. Gluck, “Introducing Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture,” Uber, 2020. Kleeman, Monzo, 2019. Lewis and Fowler, “Microservices,” 2014.
Where the cut is made decides what the rest of the system has to compensate for. Four patterns give four rules for the cut, and the same companies show more than one of them.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: The boundary inside which one model and one vocabulary stay consistent.
A system copies the communication structure of the organization that builds it.
Uber’s domain-oriented microservice architecture: services grouped into domains with one gateway each.
Team Topologies’ name for a team that owns one flow of work end to end.
How much a team must hold in its head — the limit on what it can own.
A local copy of data owned elsewhere; Netflix’s replicated in-memory store.

blocks.title: In plain words: Cut along what the business does: ordering, billing, delivery.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Cut along what the business does: ordering, billing, delivery.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The team needs a rule for what a service is, and the rule has to stay stable while the implementation changes.
💡 The pattern.
A business capability is something the business does to produce value: take orders, manage inventory, deliver, bill.
Each service corresponds to a capability. Capabilities change slowly; the code that implements them changes constantly, which is what makes them a good place for a boundary.
Amazon.

The service teams that followed the Bezos mandate were organized around what the retail business does — cataloguing, ordering, paying, fulfilling — with each team owning the service and its operation. Vogels’s “you build it, you run it” was a statement about capability ownership as much as about operations.
Netflix.

Netflix’s services follow the capabilities of a streaming business: membership and billing, playback licensing, encoding, personalization, and the device-facing API. Each is a group of services owned by a team whose name is the capability.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.
Microsoft’s .NET reference application shows the same cut at small scale. Catalog, Basket, Ordering, and Identity are four capabilities of an online shop, each a separate service with its own store.
⚠️ The cost.

Capabilities are business-level names, and a business-level name can still hide a very large service. Ordering at Amazon is not one process. The pattern gives the first cut, and the subdomain pattern refines it.

Source: Lewis and Fowler, “organized around business capabilities,” 2014. Vogels, ACM Queue, 2006. Microsoft, .NET Microservices: Architecture for Containerized .NET Applications, and the eShopOnContainers repository.

blocks.title: In plain words: Cut along the business’s own vocabulary; where a word changes meaning, a boundary is hiding.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Cut along the business’s own vocabulary; where a word changes meaning, a boundary is hiding.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A capability is too coarse, or two capabilities use the same word to mean different things, and the model inside one service is being bent to serve another.
💡 The pattern.
Domain-driven design divides the domain into subdomains — core, supporting, generic — and gives each its own bounded context with its own language.
Each bounded context is a candidate service. The same real-world thing may be a different concept in each context.
Uber, domain-oriented microservice architecture.

By 2020 Uber had about 2,200 critical microservices and the dependency graph had become the problem. DOMA groups related services into domains, gives each domain one gateway as its single entry point, arranges domains into layers (infrastructure, business, product, presentation) so that dependencies point downward, and adds an extension mechanism so a product team can extend a domain without editing its code. It is subdomain decomposition applied after the fact, to a system that had been cut by team and feature.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.

The Ordering service is a bounded context with its own language: Order, Buyer, OrderItem, PaymentMethod. The Catalog service has CatalogItem. A product is a different concept in each context. Ordering copies the name and price into the order at the moment of purchase and never joins back to the catalog table.
⚠️ The cost.
The bounded contexts exist first in a model, so a team without a model will cut by database table or by screen. Finding the contexts takes domain time that a feature deadline does not budget for.
Source: Evans, Domain-Driven Design, 2003. Gluck, Uber Engineering, 2020. Microsoft, eShopOnContainers and the .NET microservices guide, the Ordering bounded context.

blocks.title: In plain words: Draw the boundary around the people who will answer the pager.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Draw the boundary around the people who will answer the pager.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A service owned by nobody, or by everybody, is not maintained. A service owned by three teams needs a committee to change.
💡 The pattern.
The service boundary follows the team.
A small team owns one or a few services end to end, including operation. This is Conway’s law used deliberately: the communication structure of the organization becomes the structure of the system.
Amazon.
The “two-pizza team” — small enough to be fed by two pizzas — is the unit of ownership that the 2002 mandate assumed. A team owns a service, its interface, its data, and its pager.
Spotify.

Henrik Kniberg and Anders Ivarsson’s 2012 paper “Scaling Agile @ Spotify” described squads: small teams that own a feature area and the services behind it end to end, grouped into tribes. The paper became the most copied organizational diagram of the decade, and Spotify itself later said the structure was a snapshot, not a model.
Netflix.

Netflix’s 2018 “Full Cycle Developers” post states the rule directly: the team that designs and builds a service also deploys, operates, and supports it. Skelton and Pais generalized the pattern as the stream-aligned team in Team Topologies (2019), with team cognitive load as the limit on how many services one team can own.
⚠️ The cost.
Reorganizations orphan services. Service count grows with headcount rather than with the domain. A boundary drawn around a team is only as good as the team boundary was.
Source: Vogels, 2006. Kniberg and Ivarsson, “Scaling Agile @ Spotify,” 2012. Fisher-Ogden et al., “Full Cycle Developers at Netflix,” 2018. Skelton and Pais, Team Topologies, 2019.

blocks.title: In plain words: Answer the request from what you already hold; fetch nothing live from your neighbors.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Answer the request from what you already hold; fetch nothing live from your neighbors.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A request that fans out to five services synchronously has the latency of the slowest and the availability of the product of all five. Every hop is a place to time out.
💡 The pattern.
Design the service so it can answer a synchronous request without synchronously calling another service.
Data it needs from others arrives ahead of time through events and is kept locally (a CQRS view or a command-side replica). Work that must involve others is finished asynchronously through a saga.
Netflix personalization.

Netflix’s 2013 description of its recommendation architecture has three layers. Offline computation runs on Hadoop over the full history. Nearline computation runs when an event arrives and stores results. Online computation runs at request time under a strict latency budget and reads mostly precomputed rows from EVCache and
Cassandra

. The homepage request is answered from data already at hand; if the online step cannot finish in time it falls back to the precomputed result. The service that serves the page is self-contained at request time because the expensive collaboration happened before the request.
FTGO.
Chris Richardson’s worked example is the Delivery service, which keeps a replica of the restaurant and order data it needs to schedule a courier, so scheduling never waits on the Order service.
⚠️ The cost.
Replication and eventual consistency. The service answers with data that may be seconds or minutes old, and it has to be designed to say so.

Source: Amatriain and Basilico, “System Architectures for Personalization and Recommendation,” Netflix Tech Blog, 2013. Richardson, microservices.io, “Self-contained service,” and Microservices Patterns, 2018.

blocks.text: Part 3. Migrating away from a monolith

runs.t: Almost every microservice system in this document was a monolith first. Two patterns govern the years in which both exist.

blocks.alt: Part map — Migrating away from a monolith: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.
blocks.caption: Part map — Migrating away from a monolith: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: A front component that receives every request and routes it to the old or the new system.
A tree that grows around its host until the host is gone — Fowler’s metaphor.
An interface definition language: one file that describes a service’s calls, from which clients are generated.
Running the old and the new path on the same traffic and diffing the results (GitHub Scientist, Twitter Diffy).

blocks.title: In plain words: Grow the new system around the old one, route by route, until the old one can be switched off.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Grow the new system around the old one, route by route, until the old one can be switched off.

blocks.alt: A strangler fig on its host in the Anamalai hills. Netflix took from 2009 to January 2016 to strangle its data center; Airbnb began strangling Monorail in 2018. Photo: Shankar Raman, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
blocks.caption: A strangler fig on its host in the Anamalai hills. Netflix took from 2009 to January 2016 to strangle its data center; Airbnb began strangling Monorail in 2018. Photo: Shankar Raman, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

A rewrite that runs for two years and cuts over on one night has almost never worked. The old system keeps changing while the new one is built, and the cutover is the biggest release the company has ever done.
💡 The pattern.
Martin Fowler’s strangler fig (2004): the new system grows around the old one.
A facade routes each request to either the old or the new implementation. Function by function, traffic moves. The old system shrinks until it can be switched off.
Netflix.

The move to AWS took from 2009 to January 2016. Netflix moved non-member-facing systems first — encoding, then internal tools — then customer-facing pieces, and billing last, because billing had the most rules and the least tolerance for a mistake. For years the DVD business stayed in the data center while streaming ran in the cloud. Each moved piece was routed to the new implementation while the rest stayed where it was.
Airbnb.

Airbnb’s Rails monolith, “Monorail,” was strangled from 2018. Jessica Tai described the sequence: freeze new development in the monolith, extract reads before writes, move one endpoint at a time, and run the old and the new path side by side, comparing results, before switching traffic. The comparison step has its own tools: GitHub’s Scientist (2016) runs a new code path beside the old one and reports mismatches without changing the result users see, and Twitter’s Diffy (2015) replays production traffic against old and new services and diffs the responses.
⚠️ The cost.

Two systems for years, with data that has to stay in step across both. The facade is a permanent seam if the strangling stops halfway, which it often does when the visible features have moved and only the unglamorous ones remain.

Source: Fowler, “StranglerFigApplication,” 2004. Izrailevsky, Netflix, 2016. Tai, “Airbnb’s Great Migration: From Monolith to Service-Oriented,” QCon, 2018. GitHub Scientist, 2016. Twitter Diffy, 2015.

blocks.title: In plain words: A translator at the border, so the old system’s vocabulary never leaks into the new model.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
A translator at the border, so the old system’s vocabulary never leaks into the new model.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

A new service that reads the old system’s tables or speaks its API starts to think in the old system’s terms. Its model is bent to match the legacy schema, and the migration produces a second copy of the first system’s mistakes.
💡 The pattern.
Eric Evans’s anti-corruption layer (2003): a translation layer between the new model and the foreign one.
On one side it speaks the legacy system’s language; on the other it speaks the new bounded context’s. The new model never imports a legacy type.
Airbnb.

In the Monorail migration, new services were not allowed to read the monolith’s MySQL tables. A layer of data services wrapped the tables behind Thrift interfaces and owned all reads and writes to them. Domain services above depended on the Thrift interface, not on the Rails schema, so a later change of storage under a data service did not reach the callers.
Amazon.

By October 2019 Amazon’s consumer business had turned off its last Oracle database: about 7,500 databases and 75 petabytes moved to DynamoDB, Aurora, RDS, and Redshift, team by team. It was possible because, since the mandate, consumers reached a team’s data only through the team’s service interface. The interface was the layer that kept each team’s storage decision from reaching anyone else.
Payment adapters.

Every payment service that talks to Stripe, Adyen, or PayPal through an adapter is running an anti-corruption layer. The domain has its own Payment and its own state machine; the adapter translates to each provider’s objects and events.
⚠️ The cost.

Another codebase to maintain, and translation cost on every call. The layer is worth it when the foreign model is large or is going to change; for a small stable dependency, a conformist mapping is cheaper.
Source: Evans, Domain-Driven Design, 2003. Tai, QCon 2018. Barr, “Migration Complete – Amazon’s Consumer Business Just Turned off its Final Oracle Database,” AWS News Blog, 2019.

blocks.text: Part 4. Owning data and spanning services

runs.t: Once each service owns its data, one business action is no longer one database transaction. This part has the most patterns because it has the hardest problem.

blocks.alt: Part map — Owning data and spanning services: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.
blocks.caption: Part map — Owning data and spanning services: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: A protocol for one transaction across several databases — slow and usually unavailable across services.
A transaction inside one service’s own database.
The business-level undo for a completed step: a refund, not a rollback.
Cassandra’s equivalent of a database schema.
Pushing a new item into every follower’s list at write time, so reads are one fetch.
A saved point-in-time state so replaying events can start late.
A service that stores and enforces the shape of events.
A database that keeps the sequence of events as the record.

blocks.title: In plain words: Your data is yours; others ask through your API or listen to your events.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Your data is yours; others ask through your API or listen to your events.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
If two services write the same tables, a schema change by one breaks the other, the two teams have to coordinate releases, and the database is the shared bottleneck for scale.
💡 The pattern.
Each service has a private database.

Other services reach that data only through the owner’s API or its events. The store can be a separate server, a separate schema, or a separate set of tables that no one else is allowed to touch; the rule is the ownership, not the physical separation.
Amazon.

The 2002 mandate’s sharpest clause was “no direct database reads.” Seventeen years later that clause let Amazon move off Oracle team by team, with each team choosing what Vogels calls a purpose-built database: DynamoDB for key-value at scale, Aurora for relational, ElastiCache for in-memory, Redshift for analytics.
Netflix and Monzo.

Netflix services own their data in Cassandra and EVCache and expose it through APIs; there is no shared relational schema across the streaming system. Monzo runs a shared Cassandra cluster in which each service owns its own keyspace, and no service reads another service’s tables.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.

Catalog and Ordering each have their own SQL Server database, Basket uses Redis, and Identity has its own store. Each store is a separate container. The reference application shows polyglot persistence at the smallest useful scale.
⚠️ The cost.

No joins across services and no distributed transactions. Queries that used to be one SQL statement become API composition or a CQRS view. Commands that used to be one transaction become a saga. More database engines to operate.
Source: Yegge, 2011. Barr, AWS, 2019. Vogels, on purpose-built databases, re:Invent talks 2018–2019. Monzo engineering talks by Matt Heath, 2016–2018. Microsoft, eShopOnContainers.

blocks.title: In plain words: Several services write the same tables. Fast to start; the coupling arrives later.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Several services write the same tables. Fast to start; the coupling arrives later.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
Not every system is ready for private data. Early on, or when two services are tightly related, a shared schema is faster, and it keeps transactions and joins.
💡 The pattern.
Several services read and write the same database schema.
Richardson keeps it in the language as a real choice with real costs: it is the starting point for most migrations and the correct end point for some small systems.
Airbnb Monorail.

Before the SOA migration, one Rails application and one MySQL database held everything. As the first services were extracted, several of them read the same tables, and the coupling that produced is why Airbnb introduced data services as sole owners of each table group.
Shopify.

The legitimate form. Shopify’s modular monolith runs as several kinds of process — web servers, job workers — that share the shard’s MySQL. It is one codebase deployed as many processes, and the boundaries are enforced in code by Packwerk, not in the database. That is a monolith with a shared database, and it is a deliberate design.
Segment.

When Segment folded 140 destination services back into one in 2018, the services had already shared a queue and libraries. The consolidation accepted one codebase and one store rather than pretend the services were independent.
⚠️ The cost.

Schema coupling. One team’s migration breaks another team’s queries. Scaling the database is everyone’s problem. Services that share a database and deploy separately are the “distributed monolith,” which has the costs of both styles.
Source: Tai, QCon 2018. Westeinde, Shopify, 2019. Noonan, Segment, 2018. Richardson, microservices.io, “Shared database.”

blocks.title: In plain words: A long action done as a chain of small local steps, each with an undo step ready.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
A long action done as a chain of small local steps, each with an undo step ready.

blocks.alt: The saga in one picture: local transactions forward, compensations in reverse. eShop’s order saga cancels the order; Uber’s trip and Netflix’s title-launch run for hours or days.
blocks.caption: The saga in one picture: local transactions forward, compensations in reverse. eShop’s order saga cancels the order; Uber’s trip and Netflix’s title-launch run for hours or days.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

Place an order: reserve stock, charge the card, confirm. Each step is in a different service with a different database. There is no transaction that spans them, and a two-phase commit across services is unavailable or unwanted.
💡 The pattern.

Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem defined the saga in 1987 for long-lived database transactions: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating transaction that semantically undoes it.

If step four fails, compensations for steps three, two, and one run. Richardson applied the idea to services. A saga is coordinated in one of two ways, choreography or orchestration, treated in the next two chapters.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.

Placing an order is a saga across Ordering, Basket, Catalog, and Payment. The steps are local transactions in each service; if stock is rejected or payment fails, Ordering’s compensation is to move the order to Cancelled, and nothing else has to be undone because the earlier steps were designed to be reversible by that one change.
Uber and Netflix.

An Uber trip — request, match, ride, fare, charge, payout — is a long-running sequence across services with failure at every step; Uber built Cadence to run such sequences durably. A Netflix title going live — ingest, encode, quality-check, publish — is a saga across media services, and Netflix built Conductor to coordinate it.
⚠️ The cost.

Compensations are business logic and have to be designed: a refund is not a rollback. Sagas lack isolation, so another saga can read data a saga is about to compensate. Richardson lists the countermeasures — semantic lock, commutative updates, pessimistic view, re-read value — and each is more code.
Source: Garcia-Molina and Salem, “Sagas,” SIGMOD 1987. Richardson, Microservices Patterns, chapter 4. Microsoft, eShopOnContainers. Uber Cadence, 2017. Netflix Conductor, 2016.

blocks.title: In plain words: No conductor: each service reacts to the last event and publishes the next.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
No conductor: each service reacts to the last event and publishes the next.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The saga needs coordination, and the team does not want a coordinator that every service depends on.
💡 The pattern.
Each service does its local transaction and publishes an event.
The next service subscribes to that event and reacts. No one holds the whole workflow; it exists only as the sum of the subscriptions.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.

The order saga is documented event by event. Ordering saves the order and publishes OrderStartedIntegrationEvent; Basket deletes the buyer’s basket. Ordering publishes OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent; Catalog checks stock and publishes OrderStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent or OrderStockRejectedIntegrationEvent; Ordering moves the order to StockConfirmed or Cancelled. Ordering publishes OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent; Payment charges and publishes OrderPaymentSucceededIntegrationEvent or OrderPaymentFailedIntegrationEvent; Ordering marks the order Paid or Cancelled, and on Paid, Catalog decrements stock. Every arrow is a subscription. There is no service called OrderProcess.
LinkedIn.

Kafka was built at LinkedIn in 2010 to carry exactly this style at company scale. A member edits a profile; the change is published once; search indexing, the news feed, and the Hadoop pipeline each consume it and react independently. Jay Kreps’s 2013 essay “The Log” is the argument for the event log as the coordination medium.
⚠️ The cost.

The workflow is nowhere to read. To know where an order is, an engineer follows a correlation ID through six services’ logs. Cyclic subscriptions appear by accident. Adding a step means changing which events are consumed in several services.

Source: Microsoft, .NET microservices guide, “Implementing event-based communication between microservices,” and the eShopOnContainers integration events. Kreps, “The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data’s unifying abstraction,” 2013.

blocks.title: In plain words: One conductor tells each service what to do, and runs the undo steps when something fails.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
One conductor tells each service what to do, and runs the undo steps when something fails.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The saga has many steps, branches, and compensations, and the team needs to see the workflow as one thing and know exactly where each instance is.
💡 The pattern.
One orchestrator holds the workflow.
It tells each participant what to do next, waits for the reply, and on failure runs the compensations in reverse order. Participants stay simple; the orchestrator holds the state.
Netflix Conductor.

Open-sourced in December 2016 to run Netflix’s content ingestion and media processing workflows. A workflow is a JSON definition of tasks with fork, join, decision, and sub-workflow; worker services poll for their task type, do the work, and report back; the server tracks state, retries, and timeouts, and a failed workflow can be restarted from the failed task. Netflix stepped back from the project in 2023 and the community continued it as Conductor OSS and Orkes.
Uber Cadence and Temporal.

Cadence (2017) took a different shape: the orchestrator is ordinary code — a “workflow function” in Go or Java — and the platform makes it durable by recording every decision as an event and replaying the history to recover state after a crash. A workflow can sleep for thirty days and wake up. Its creators, Maxim Fateev and Samar Abbas, forked it as Temporal in 2019. AWS Step Functions (2016) is the managed version of the same idea with a state-machine definition.
FTGO.

Richardson’s CreateOrderSaga is the small worked case: the orchestrator sends commands to Consumer, Kitchen, and Accounting services and runs RejectTicket and other compensations when a step replies with failure.
⚠️ The cost.

The orchestrator can become the place where all business logic ends up — the smart pipe that the 2014 article warned against — and a single point that every participant depends on. In exchange, the workflow is explicit, its state is queryable, and the compensation order is written down.
Source: Netflix Conductor, 2016, and the 2023 transition note. Uber Engineering on Cadence, 2017–2020; Temporal, 2019. AWS Step Functions, 2016. Richardson, Microservices Patterns, chapter 4.

blocks.title: In plain words: Keep a local copy of the other team’s facts, refreshed by their events, so you never call them mid-action.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Keep a local copy of the other team’s facts, refreshed by their events, so you never call them mid-action.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A command in one service needs data another service owns — the price of an item, a customer’s credit limit — and the team does not want a synchronous call on the command path.
💡 The pattern.
The service that performs the command keeps a read-only replica of the data it must see, updated by subscribing to the owner’s events.
The command reads the local copy.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.

Catalog owns prices. When a price changes, Catalog publishes ProductPriceChangedIntegrationEvent. Basket subscribes and updates the price of that product in every stored basket in Redis. When the customer adds an item or checks out, Basket uses the price it holds and never calls Catalog. The basket is a command-side replica of catalog prices, maintained by events.
Netflix EVCache.

Netflix keeps member, entitlement, and personalization data in EVCache, a replicated in-memory store built on memcached, near the services that need it, and since 2016 replicates writes across AWS regions so that a service in any region reads its copy locally. Playback and homepage services read the replica instead of calling the owning service on every request.
⚠️ The cost.

Staleness — the replica can lag the owner by the event delay. The replicating service depends on the owner’s event schema. Data is stored twice, and the replica has to be rebuilt if events were missed.

Source: Microsoft, eShopOnContainers, Basket service and the ProductPriceChangedIntegrationEvent handler. Netflix Tech Blog, “Announcing EVCache,” 2013, and “Caching for a Global Netflix,” 2016. Richardson, microservices.io, “Command-side replica.”

blocks.title: In plain words: Ask everyone who owns a piece of the answer, then join the pieces in memory.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Ask everyone who owns a piece of the answer, then join the pieces in memory.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A query needs data from several services — the order, the customer, the delivery status — and there is no database to join them in.
💡 The pattern.
A composer calls each service that owns part of the answer and joins the results in memory.
The composer can be the client, an API gateway, or a dedicated service.
Amazon.

Vogels’s 2006 description of a product page: a request draws on more than a hundred services — pricing, availability, reviews, recommendations, images — and the page is composed from their answers. The page renderer is the composer.
Netflix API.

Daniel Jacobson’s 2012–2013 posts describe the Netflix API tier: a device request fans out to dozens of backend services and is composed into one response shaped for that device. Hystrix was born in this tier, because a composer that calls forty services meets every one of their failures. In 2020 Netflix moved the composition to GraphQL Federation: each team runs a Domain Graph Service that owns part of the schema, and a federated gateway plans the query, calls the services, and joins the results. The composer became a query planner.
⚠️ The cost.

In-memory joins over large results do not scale. The composer is on the critical path of every downstream failure and needs timeouts and fallbacks. Fan-out latency is the slowest call, not the average.
Source: Vogels, ACM Queue, 2006. Jacobson, “Embracing the Differences: Inside the Netflix API Redesign,” 2012. Netflix Tech Blog, “How Netflix Scales its API with GraphQL Federation,” 2020.

blocks.title: In plain words: One model for changing things; a separate, pre-shaped view for reading them.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
One model for changing things; a separate, pre-shaped view for reading them.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The read shape and the write shape are different. Writes need the aggregate and its rules; reads need a flat view, often across several owners, and they happen a hundred times more often.
💡 The pattern.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation.

Commands go through the domain model and update the service’s database. A separate query model — one or more views — is maintained from the events that commands produce, and queries read the view. The two models can share a database or be separate stores.
Twitter.

Raffi Krikorian’s 2012 “Timelines at Scale” is the industrial case. The write path takes a tweet and fans it out into the Redis timeline list of every follower — fanout on write. The read path for a home timeline is one Redis fetch of that list plus hydration of the tweets. The list is a read model maintained by the fanout service; the tweet store is the write model. Users with millions of followers were handled differently, because fanning out to millions of lists for one tweet does not pay.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.

The simplified form. Ordering’s commands go through the Order aggregate with Entity Framework Core; its queries are plain SQL through Dapper against the same database, returning view models directly. No second store, but two models.
Airbnb.
In the SOA migration, “derived data services” were read models: they combined data from several data services, kept their own storage, and were updated from change events captured by SpinalTap.
⚠️ The cost.

The view lags the write. A user who posts and immediately reads may not see their own write unless the design handles it. Views have to be rebuilt when their shape changes, which means replaying events.

Source: Krikorian, “Timelines at Scale,” QCon SF 2012. Microsoft, .NET microservices guide, “Applying CQRS and CQS approaches in a DDD microservice.” Tai, QCon 2018. Airbnb, “Capturing Data Evolution in a Service-Oriented Architecture,” 2018.

blocks.title: In plain words: Announce what happened; let whoever cares react.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Announce what happened; let whoever cares react.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
Something meaningful happened inside a service — an order was paid, a delivery was completed — and other services need to know, without the owner knowing who they are.
💡 The pattern.
The service publishes an event whenever its data changes in a way the business names.
The event carries the identity of the aggregate and what happened. Subscribers react; the publisher does not wait for them.
Stripe.

Every change to a Stripe object produces an Event: charge.succeeded, invoice.paid, customer.subscription.deleted. Events are stored, listed through the Events API, and delivered to customers’ endpoints by webhooks. It is a domain-event feed exposed as a product, and it is why an integrator can build a whole billing workflow without polling.
Shopify.
Shopify webhook topics — orders/create, products/update, app/uninstalled — are the same shape, and the app ecosystem is built on them.
Zalando Nakadi.

Inside a company the same idea needs a bus. Zalando’s Nakadi (2016) is an event broker with a RESTful API and a schema registry: a team registers an event type with a JSON schema, publishes events that are validated against it, and other teams subscribe. The schema enforcement is what makes the event a contract rather than a log line.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.

The distinction that matters inside one service: OrderStartedDomainEvent is handled in-process through MediatR by other aggregates in the same model; OrderStartedIntegrationEvent is the version that leaves the service on the bus. Two events, two audiences.
⚠️ The cost.
The event schema is a public contract and has to be versioned like an API. The publisher acquires consumers it does not know about, and removing a field becomes a negotiation.
Source: Stripe API reference, Events and Webhooks. Shopify Admin API, webhook topics. Zalando Nakadi, 2016. Microsoft, eShopOnContainers, domain events versus integration events.

blocks.title: In plain words: Store the history of changes, not just the latest state, and rebuild state by replaying it.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Store the history of changes, not just the latest state, and rebuild state by replaying it.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

The current row says what the balance is. It does not say how it got there, and the business or the regulator wants to know. Audit, replay, and temporal queries are afterthoughts in a state-based store.
💡 The pattern.
The service stores an aggregate as the sequence of events that produced it, appended to an event store, and rebuilds current state by replaying them.
Snapshots shorten the replay. The event log is the source of truth; every other representation is derived.
LMAX.

Martin Fowler’s 2011 description of the LMAX exchange: the business logic processor is a single-threaded in-memory Java object. Every input event is journaled to disk before it is processed, replicas process the same journal, and after a restart the processor is rebuilt from a snapshot plus the events since. The journal is the database. The design allowed six million orders per second on one thread with the Disruptor ring buffer feeding it.
Netflix Downloads.

Netflix’s 2017 “Scaling Event Sourcing for Netflix Downloads” describes the license service for offline viewing. Every license event — granted, renewed, released — is appended to Cassandra; the aggregate is rebuilt in memory from its events; snapshots are taken to bound replay time. The posts are candid about the costs: evolving event schemas, and testing that old events still replay correctly against new code.
Kafka.

LinkedIn’s Kafka is a durable, replayable log, and Kreps’s “The Log” argues that the whole company’s state can be treated as derived from it. Kafka is not an event store for aggregates, but it made replayable logs an ordinary component.
⚠️ The cost.

Event schema evolution is permanent: an event written in 2017 must still replay in 2026. Queries need projections, so event sourcing almost always brings CQRS. The mental model is unfamiliar to most teams.

Source: Fowler, “The LMAX Architecture,” 2011. Avery and Reta, “Scaling Event Sourcing for Netflix Downloads,” Netflix Tech Blog, 2017. Kreps, “The Log,” 2013. Greg Young on CQRS and event sourcing, 2010–2012.

blocks.text: Part 5. Publishing a message with the database write

runs.t: A service writes an order and then publishes OrderPlaced. If it crashes between the two, the order exists and no one knows. Three patterns close the gap.

blocks.alt: Part map — Publishing a message with the database write: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.
blocks.caption: Part map — Publishing a message with the database write: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: A message may arrive more than once, never zero times.
Reading a database’s own change log and publishing the changes.
MySQL’s and Postgres’s durable records of every change.
Asking again and again on a timer.

blocks.title: In plain words: Write the outgoing message into your own database with the data; a helper delivers it later, so nothing is lost.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Write the outgoing message into your own database with the data; a helper delivers it later, so nothing is lost.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

The database write commits and the publish to the broker fails, or the reverse. There is no transaction that spans a database and a message broker, and two-phase commit is not on offer from Kafka or RabbitMQ.
💡 The pattern.
The service writes the business row and a row in an outbox table in the same local transaction.
A separate publisher reads the outbox and sends the messages. Because both rows commit or neither does, the message can never be lost, only delayed or duplicated.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.

The IntegrationEventLogEF library is an outbox. When Ordering saves an order, it also inserts an IntegrationEventLogEntry into an event log table in the same database, inside the same Entity Framework transaction. After commit, the integration event service publishes the pending entries to RabbitMQ or Azure Service Bus and marks each Published; a failed publish leaves the entry marked for retry. The guide explains the reason in one sentence: the update and the event must succeed or fail together.
Debezium.

Gunnar Morling’s 2019 outbox event router made the pattern infrastructure. The service writes the outbox row in its transaction; Debezium tails the database log, picks up the outbox insert, and routes it to a Kafka topic named in the row; the service can delete the outbox row immediately, because Debezium has already read the insert from the log. The publisher in the pattern is replaced by change data capture.
⚠️ The cost.

At-least-once delivery, so every consumer has to be idempotent. The outbox table grows and needs cleanup. There is a delay between commit and publish equal to the publisher’s polling or tailing interval.

Source: Microsoft, .NET microservices guide, “Designing atomicity and resiliency when publishing to the event bus,” and the IntegrationEventLogEF project. Morling, “Reliable Microservices Data Exchange With the Outbox Pattern,” Debezium blog, 2019. Richardson, microservices.io, “Transactional outbox.”

blocks.title: In plain words: Read the database’s own change log and turn each change into a message.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Read the database’s own change log and turn each change into a message.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The team wants every committed change published without touching application code, and without a polling query hammering the outbox table.
💡 The pattern.
A process reads the database’s own transaction log — MySQL’s binlog, Postgres’s write-ahead log, the Oracle redo log — and publishes each change it finds.
The database already recorded the change durably; the tailer turns that record into a message.
LinkedIn Databus.

Databus (published 2012, open-sourced 2013) captured changes from LinkedIn’s Oracle and MySQL databases and fed them, in commit order, to search indexes, the social graph, and caches. It is the direct ancestor of every change-data-capture system in this chapter.
Debezium, SpinalTap, DBLog, Wormhole.

Debezium (Red Hat, 2016) reads MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB, SQL Server, and Oracle logs into Kafka and is the open-source default. Airbnb’s SpinalTap (2018) reads MySQL binlogs and DynamoDB streams into Kafka and drives search indexing, cache invalidation, and derived data. Netflix’s DBLog (2019) adds a way to take a consistent full snapshot while the log keeps flowing, so a new consumer can bootstrap. Facebook’s Wormhole (2015) is the same mechanic over the MySQL binlog at Facebook scale, feeding caches and indexes across regions.
⚠️ The cost.

Coupled to one database engine’s log format. A row change is not a domain event: “orders.status changed from 2 to 3” has to be turned into OrderPaid somewhere, which is why the outbox and CDC are usually combined. Snapshot and ordering semantics need care.

Source: Das et al., “All Aboard the Databus!,” SoCC 2012. Debezium, 2016. Airbnb, “Capturing Data Evolution in a Service-Oriented Architecture,” 2018. Andreakis and Papapanagiotou, “DBLog: A Generic Change-Data-Capture Framework,” Netflix, 2019. Sharma et al., “Wormhole,” NSDI 2015.

blocks.title: In plain words: A loop that checks for unsent rows and sends them. Plain, a little slow, works anywhere.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
A loop that checks for unsent rows and sends them. Plain, a little slow, works anywhere.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The team has an outbox or an event table and needs the simplest possible thing that publishes it.
💡 The pattern.
A process polls the table for rows not yet published, publishes them, and marks them sent.
No log access, no broker transaction, no special database features.
Eventuate Tram.
Richardson’s framework for the
FTGO

example publishes the outbox either by polling or by tailing the log, and polling is the default when the database does not expose its log. The polling loop is a SELECT of unpublished rows, a publish, and an UPDATE.
Stripe webhooks.

Stripe stores every event and delivers it to each subscribed endpoint. A failed delivery is retried with exponential backoff for up to three days in live mode. The delivery system is a publisher working through a stored table of pending deliveries; the event store is the outbox, and the retry schedule is the polling interval.
Database-backed job queues.

Rails’ Delayed Job and Solid Queue, and Sidekiq’s Postgres-backed cousins, are polled tables of work. Used to carry publish jobs, they are polling publishers by another name, and many teams have one without calling it that.
⚠️ The cost.
Polling adds load and a latency floor equal to the interval. Concurrent publishers need row locking or partitioning. In return it runs anywhere.
Source: Richardson, Eventuate Tram documentation and microservices.io, “Polling publisher.” Stripe documentation, webhook delivery and retry behavior.

The 2014 article asked for smart endpoints and dumb pipes. The pipes in popular software are two: request-response, and messages through a broker. Two smaller patterns cover protocols built for a domain and what happens when a message arrives twice.

blocks.alt: Part map — Communicating between services: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.
blocks.caption: Part map — Communicating between services: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: A formal description of calls or messages from which code is generated.
The newer web protocol gRPC rides on: multiplexed, binary, efficient.
The middleman that stores and forwards messages (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS).
One publishes; any number subscribe and receive.
Lightweight publish-subscribe and chat protocols older than smartphones.
A client-chosen identifier that makes a retried request safe.

blocks.title: In plain words: Call and wait for the answer — a phone call between services.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Call and wait for the answer — a phone call between services.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
One service needs an answer from another now: is this item in stock, what is this customer’s address.
💡 The pattern.
The caller sends a request and blocks for the response.
The interface is defined in a schema or an IDL, and clients are generated. HTTP with JSON, gRPC, and Thrift are the common forms.
Google gRPC.

Google’s internal RPC system, Stubby, connected every service in the company for a decade before Google released gRPC in 2015 (1.0 in 2016): HTTP/2 transport, Protocol Buffers as the schema, generated clients in a dozen languages, and deadlines and cancellation built into every call. It became the default for service-to-service calls in the Kubernetes ecosystem.
Facebook Thrift.

Facebook built Thrift in 2007 so services written in PHP, C++, Java, and Python could call each other through one IDL; it went to Apache. Airbnb chose Thrift IDL for its SOA in 2018 for the same reason: one definition, generated clients in Ruby and Java.
Twitter Finagle.

Finagle (2011) is an RPC system where a service is a function from request to future response; load balancing, retries, timeouts, and Zipkin tracing are composable filters around that function. It carried Twitter’s traffic and is the ancestor of Linkerd.
⚠️ The cost.
Temporal coupling: both services must be up at the same moment. Failure cascades along the call chain, which is why discovery, breakers, and timeouts follow in later parts.
Source: gRPC, 2015–2016. Slee, Agarwal, and Kwiatkowski, “Thrift: Scalable Cross-Language Services Implementation,” Facebook, 2007. Eriksen, “Your Server as a Function,” PLOS 2013. Tai, QCon 2018.

blocks.title: In plain words: Leave a message in a mailbox; the receiver reads it when ready.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Leave a message in a mailbox; the receiver reads it when ready.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The sender should not have to wait for, or even know about, the receiver. Work should survive a receiver being down. Load should be smoothed rather than propagated.
💡 The pattern.
Services exchange messages through a broker.
Point-to-point channels carry commands; publish-subscribe channels carry events. The broker stores the message until a consumer takes it.
LinkedIn Kafka.

Kafka was built at LinkedIn in 2010 to replace a tangle of point-to-point feeds with one partitioned, replicated log that many consumers read at their own pace. It was open-sourced in 2011 and became the event backbone of most large microservice systems, including Netflix, Uber, and Airbnb.
Amazon SQS.

Simple Queue Service was the first AWS service released to the public, in beta in 2004 and generally available in 2006, before EC2. Amazon shipped a queue before it shipped a computer, which says what it thought the hard part of a distributed system was.
Netflix Keystone and RabbitMQ.

Netflix’s Keystone pipeline carried hundreds of billions of events a day through Kafka by 2016. At the small end, eShopOnContainers uses RabbitMQ as its default event bus, with Azure Service Bus as the alternative implementation behind the same interface.
⚠️ The cost.

At-least-once delivery, out-of-order arrival, and a broker to operate. Debugging an asynchronous flow needs correlation IDs and tracing. The broker invites logic into the pipe — routing rules, transformations — which the 2014 article said belongs in the endpoints.

Source: Kreps, Narkhede, and Rao, “Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing,” 2011. Amazon Web Services announcements, 2004 and 2006. Netflix Tech Blog, “Evolution of the Netflix Data Pipeline,” 2016. Microsoft, eShopOnContainers event bus.

blocks.title: In plain words: When HTTP is the wrong shape, speak a language built for the job: chat, telephony, devices.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
When HTTP is the wrong shape, speak a language built for the job: chat, telephony, devices.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
HTTP request-response fits ordering a book. It fits badly when the connection must stay open, messages are tiny and frequent, and the client is a phone on a weak network.
💡 The pattern.
Services and clients speak a protocol built for the domain instead of a general HTTP or messaging API.
Email has SMTP, telephony has SIP, databases have wire protocols. Chat, presence, and telemetry get protocols of their own.
Facebook Messenger.

Facebook’s 2011 engineering note on building Messenger explains that HTTP’s overhead made low-latency mobile messaging impractical, so the phone client speaks MQTT — a 1999 publish-subscribe protocol designed at IBM for constrained devices — over a persistent connection to Facebook’s servers.
WhatsApp and Discord.

WhatsApp’s clients speak a modified, compressed XMPP, the chat protocol standardized in the early 2000s, to an Erlang backend. Discord’s clients hold a WebSocket to the Gateway and exchange framed messages with opcodes for heartbeat, identify, and event dispatch; REST is used only for actions that fit it.
⚠️ The cost.
Bespoke tooling. Generic gateways, tracers, and load balancers understand HTTP and gRPC; a domain protocol needs its own.

Source: Zhang, “Building Facebook Messenger,” Facebook Engineering, 2011. MQTT, Stanford-Clark and Nipper, 1999. WhatsApp engineering talks by Rick Reed, 2012–2014. Discord developer documentation, Gateway.

blocks.title: In plain words: Getting the same message twice must have the same effect as getting it once.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Getting the same message twice must have the same effect as getting it once.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
Brokers and retries deliver at least once. A payment handler that receives ChargeCard twice charges twice.
💡 The pattern.
A handler can receive the same message more than once and produce exactly one effect.
Either the operation is naturally idempotent (set status to Paid), or the handler records the message ID it has processed, in the same transaction as the business change, and ignores repeats.
Stripe.

Brandur Leach’s 2017 post on Stripe’s idempotency keys is the reference design. A client puts an Idempotency-Key header on a POST; Stripe stores the key with the outcome of the first request for 24 hours and returns that stored result to any retry, so a network failure after the charge does not produce a second charge. The client library retries freely because the key makes the retry safe.
Kafka and SQS.

Kafka 0.11 (2017) added the idempotent producer — a producer ID and sequence number let the broker discard duplicates from a retried send — and transactions across partitions. Amazon SQS FIFO queues (2016) deduplicate on a MessageDeduplicationId within a five-minute window. Both make the pipe help, and neither removes the need for the handler to be safe on its own.
Eventuate Tram.
Richardson’s framework keeps a received_messages table; the handler inserts the message ID in the same transaction as its business update, and a duplicate fails the insert and is skipped.
⚠️ The cost.
Storage for processed IDs and a policy for how long to keep them. Choosing what the key is — the request, the business action, the message — is a design decision the team has to make on purpose.
Source: Leach, “Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency,” Stripe, 2017. KIP-98, Apache Kafka 0.11, 2017. Amazon SQS FIFO, 2016. Richardson, microservices.io, “Idempotent consumer.”
A phone should not know that there are four hundred services. Two patterns put a front door in place.

blocks.alt: Part map — Facing external clients: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.
blocks.caption: Part map — Facing external clients: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: Decrypting incoming HTTPS at the edge.
Refusing requests beyond an agreed pace.
Combining several backend calls into one response.
Handling many connections without a thread waiting on each.

blocks.title: In plain words: One front door that knows the way to every room.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
One front door that knows the way to every room.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
Clients would otherwise call many services directly, know their addresses, handle each one’s authentication, and make a dozen round trips over a mobile network for one screen.
💡 The pattern.
One entry service receives all external requests.
It routes to internal services, authenticates, rate-limits, and often aggregates several calls into one response. Internal topology is hidden behind it.
Netflix Zuul.

Zuul (open-sourced 2013) fronts all Netflix device traffic. Filters written in Groovy run at request time for authentication, routing, canary release, and load shedding, and can be changed without redeploying the gateway. Zuul 2 (2018) rebuilt it on Netty for asynchronous, non-blocking I/O to handle connection spikes when millions of devices reconnect at once.
Amazon API Gateway and Kong.

Amazon API Gateway (2015) is the managed form: routes, throttling, keys, and authorizers in front of Lambda functions and services. Kong (2015) is the open-source form on NGINX and OpenResty with plugins for the same jobs.
Uber.

Uber’s 2020 description of its API gateway: the edge layer terminates TLS, authenticates, translates protocols, applies rate limits, and exposes thousands of endpoints defined in configuration, so product teams publish an endpoint without writing gateway code.
⚠️ The cost.
One more hop, a component every request depends on, and a team that owns it. A gateway attracts business logic and becomes the smart pipe; the backend-for-frontend pattern is one answer to that.
Source: Netflix Tech Blog, “Announcing Zuul,” 2013, and “Open Sourcing Zuul 2,” 2018. Amazon API Gateway, 2015. Kong, 2015. Thangavelu et al., “The Architecture of Uber’s API Gateway,” 2020.

blocks.title: In plain words: A front door per kind of client, owned by that client’s team.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
A front door per kind of client, owned by that client’s team.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
One gateway serving web, iOS, Android, and TV becomes a bottleneck: every client team files changes against it, and the response shape is a compromise that fits none of them.
💡 The pattern.
A separate backend per client experience, owned by the team that ships that client.
Each composes and shapes responses for its own screens. One experience, one backend.
SoundCloud.

Phil Calçado described the practice at SoundCloud, where the single public API shared by all clients had become the place every team waited on. Each client team got its own backend, deployed on its own schedule, that called the internal services and returned exactly what its screens needed. Sam Newman wrote the pattern up in 2015, adding REA Group as a second case.
Netflix.

Netflix reached the same shape from inside its API tier. In 2013 Jacobson described the “client adapter layer”: device teams wrote Groovy scripts, deployed into the API service without an API-team release, that shaped the generic response for their device. The scripts were backends for frontends living inside one process.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.
The reference application has a web shopping aggregator and a mobile shopping aggregator behind Envoy, each composing Catalog, Basket, and Ordering calls for its client.
⚠️ The cost.
Duplication across the backends and more deployables. The pattern works only while the rule holds: one experience, one backend. A backend shared by two clients is a gateway again.
Source: Newman, “Pattern: Backends For Frontends,” 2015, citing Calçado’s SoundCloud work. Jacobson, “The Netflix Dynamic Scripting Platform,” 2013. Microsoft, eShopOnContainers aggregators.
Instances start, stop, and move. A caller needs a current address. Five patterns split the work between the caller, a router, a registry, and whoever fills the registry.

blocks.alt: Part map — Finding a service instance: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.
blocks.caption: Part map — Finding a service instance: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: A periodic ‘still alive’ signal; the registry evicts an entry whose lease expires.
The name-to-address system; a stable name in front of moving instances.
Kubernetes’ list of the ready pod addresses behind a Service.
Kernel rules that forward a virtual address to a real one.
Keep answering with possibly stale data, or refuse to answer rather than be wrong.

blocks.title: In plain words: The caller opens the address book and picks an instance itself.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
The caller opens the address book and picks an instance itself.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A load balancer in front of every service is another hop, another component, and another team’s configuration change for every new service.
💡 The pattern.
The caller asks a service registry for the instances of the service it wants, chooses one with its own load-balancing logic, and calls it directly.
Netflix Eureka and Ribbon.

Eureka (2012) is the registry; Ribbon is the client. A Netflix service fetches the registry, caches it, and load-balances across instances itself, preferring instances in its own availability zone. Because the client holds a cached copy, a Eureka outage does not stop calls — the cache goes stale but keeps working, a deliberate choice for availability over consistency. Spring Cloud Netflix (2015) brought the pair to the wider JVM world.
gRPC.

gRPC clients can load-balance across a list of addresses supplied by a resolver, and with the xDS protocol from the Envoy project can receive that list from a control plane — client-side discovery with a mesh-style source of truth.
⚠️ The cost.
Discovery and load-balancing logic in every language the company uses. Netflix could do it because it was a JVM shop; Prana was built for everyone else.
Source: Netflix Tech Blog, “Netflix Shares Cloud Load Balancing and Failover Tool: Eureka!,” 2012. Spring Cloud Netflix, 2015. gRPC xDS support, 2020.

blocks.title: In plain words: The caller sends to one stable name; a router picks the instance.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
The caller sends to one stable name; a router picks the instance.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The team wants discovery out of the application code and the same for every language.
💡 The pattern.
The caller sends to a stable address — a load balancer or a virtual IP.
The router queries the registry and forwards to a healthy instance. The caller knows only the name.
Kubernetes.

A Service is a stable DNS name and cluster IP. kube-proxy programs iptables or IPVS rules on every node so that traffic to the cluster IP is forwarded to one of the ready pods listed in the Service’s EndpointSlices. The calling pod resolves a name and connects; it never sees a pod IP change.
AWS ELB and Airbnb SmartStack.

Elastic Load Balancing (2009) with Auto Scaling groups was the cloud’s first version of the pattern, and it is how Netflix exposed services to the edge. Airbnb’s SmartStack (2013) put the router on each host: Synapse configures a local HAProxy with one port per dependency, and the application connects to localhost. The registry is ZooKeeper, filled by Nerve.
⚠️ The cost.
One more hop, and a router that is itself a critical component to scale and secure. In Kubernetes the hop is a kernel rule; in a hardware balancer it is a device.
Source: Kubernetes documentation, Services and kube-proxy. AWS Elastic Load Balancing, 2009. Serebryany, “SmartStack: Service Discovery in the Cloud,” Airbnb, 2013.

blocks.title: In plain words: The address book: who is running where, and whether they are healthy.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
The address book: who is running where, and whether they are healthy.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
Someone has to hold the current list of instances and their health, and stay available while instances churn.
💡 The pattern.
A database of service instances and their network locations.
Instances or a registrar write to it; clients or routers read from it. It is the one component in this part that everyone depends on.
Eureka.

A peer-replicated registry that chose availability over consistency: each Eureka server holds the full registry, replicates to peers, and keeps serving from its copy if peers are unreachable. Instances that stop heart-beating are evicted after a lease expires.
ZooKeeper, Consul, etcd.

Yahoo’s ZooKeeper (2008) was the consistent coordination store that Airbnb’s SmartStack and Twitter’s Finagle ServerSets used as a registry, and that Kafka used until KRaft. HashiCorp Consul (2014) combined a registry, health checks, a key-value store, and a DNS interface, so any client that can resolve a name can discover. Kubernetes stores its Services and EndpointSlices in etcd (2013), which makes etcd the registry for every Kubernetes cluster without anyone calling it that.
⚠️ The cost.
The registry’s consistency choice becomes the system’s. Eureka may hand out a dead address for up to ninety seconds; ZooKeeper may refuse to answer during a partition. Both are correct for someone.

Source: Netflix Eureka wiki. Hunt et al., “ZooKeeper: Wait-free coordination for Internet-scale systems,” USENIX ATC 2010. HashiCorp Consul, 2014. etcd, CoreOS, 2013; Kubernetes architecture documentation.

blocks.title: In plain words: Each instance writes itself into the address book when it starts.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Each instance writes itself into the address book when it starts.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The registry is empty until something fills it.
💡 The pattern.
Each service instance registers itself on startup, sends heartbeats while it runs, and deregisters on shutdown.
The service knows best when it is ready.
Eureka.

A Eureka client registers on start, renews its lease every thirty seconds, and is evicted if no renewal arrives for ninety seconds. A Spring Boot application with the Eureka client on its classpath does all of this with one annotation; the registration code is in the library, not the service.
Consul and Twitter.

A Consul agent runs on each host and the service registers with the local agent, which reports to the cluster and runs the health checks. Twitter’s Finagle services announced themselves into ZooKeeper ServerSets, and clients resolved a service name to the current set.
⚠️ The cost.
Registration code in every service or every chassis. A process that crashes without deregistering leaves a stale entry until the lease expires, so callers must tolerate a dead address.
Source: Netflix Eureka wiki, client configuration. HashiCorp Consul, service registration. Twitter Finagle, ServerSets and Zookeeper.

blocks.title: In plain words: Someone else — usually the platform — writes the instance into the address book.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Someone else — usually the platform — writes the instance into the address book.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The service is written in a language without a registry client, or the team wants the platform to own registration so the service does not have to.
💡 The pattern.
A registrar registers and deregisters instances on their behalf, by watching the platform or by probing the process.
The service is unaware of the registry.
Kubernetes.

A pod does nothing to be discovered. The kubelet reports the pod’s readiness; the EndpointSlice controller in the control plane watches pods that match a Service’s selector and writes their IPs into the Service’s EndpointSlices when they are ready, and removes them when they are not. Registration is a side effect of scheduling.
Netflix Prana, Airbnb Nerve, Registrator.

Prana (2014) is a sidecar that registers a non-JVM process with Eureka and heartbeats for it. Airbnb’s Nerve runs on each host, health-checks each local service, and writes its presence into ZooKeeper. Glider Labs’ Registrator (2014) watches Docker container start and stop events and registers them with Consul or etcd. Each is a registrar standing beside a service that never heard of the registry.
⚠️ The cost.
The registrar has to know whether the service is healthy, which is why third-party registration and the health check API arrive together.

Source: Kubernetes documentation, EndpointSlices and readiness. Netflix Tech Blog, “Prana: A Sidecar for your Netflix PaaS based Applications and Services,” 2014. Serebryany, Airbnb, 2013. Glider Labs Registrator, 2014.

In a monolith a slow function slows the process. In a service system a slow dependency exhausts the caller’s threads, then the caller’s callers. Michael Nygard named the defenses in Release It! (2007), and Netflix turned them into a library.

blocks.alt: Part map — Containing failure: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.
blocks.caption: Part map — Containing failure: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: A fixed set of workers; exhaust it and every caller waits.
The breaker’s trial state: let one call through to see if the dependency recovered.
Passing ‘how much time is left’ down the call chain.
Random spread added to retry delays so a fleet does not retry in lockstep.
A cap on retries as a share of requests, so retries cannot cause an outage.
A complete copy of a service serving a slice of customers, so a failure is bounded.

blocks.title: In plain words: After too many failures, stop calling for a while; test the water before resuming.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
After too many failures, stop calling for a while; test the water before resuming.

blocks.alt: Household circuit breakers: they trip to protect the wiring. Hystrix opened its circuit at a 50 percent failure rate over ten seconds and let one trial call through after five. Photo: Bidgee, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
blocks.caption: Household circuit breakers: they trip to protect the wiring. Hystrix opened its circuit at a 50 percent failure rate over ten seconds and let one trial call through after five. Photo: Bidgee, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A dependency is failing. Every call to it still takes the full timeout, still holds a thread, and still fails. The caller spends its capacity waiting for a service that cannot answer.
💡 The pattern.
A proxy counts failures.

When the failure rate over a window crosses a threshold, the circuit opens and calls fail immediately without being attempted. After a pause the circuit goes half-open and lets a trial call through; success closes it. Nygard’s metaphor is the electrical breaker: it trips to protect the wiring.
Netflix Hystrix.

Hystrix (2012) wraps each dependency call in a command. With default settings, the circuit opens when at least 20 requests in a rolling ten-second window have a failure rate above 50 percent, stays open for five seconds, and then tries one request. Each command has a fallback — a cached value, a default, an empty list — so the Netflix API tier degraded a row of the homepage rather than the page. Netflix reported tens of billions of thread-isolated calls a day through Hystrix. It entered maintenance in 2018, with Resilience4j recommended in its place, and its dashboard of open and closed circuits is still the mental image most engineers have of the pattern.
Polly and Envoy.

eShopOnContainers uses Polly, the .NET resilience library, to put a breaker around each HttpClient. Envoy’s outlier detection does the same job in the proxy: hosts that return consecutive 5xx responses are ejected from the load-balancing pool for a period and then readmitted, and Istio exposes it as a DestinationRule. The breaker moved from a library in the service to a sidecar beside it.
⚠️ The cost.

Thresholds have to be tuned per dependency; under low traffic the sample is too small and the breaker flaps. A fallback is business logic — what does the page show when recommendations are down — and has to be designed.

Source: Nygard, Release It!, 2007. Netflix Tech Blog, “Introducing Hystrix for Resilience Engineering,” 2012; Hystrix wiki, configuration defaults; maintenance announcement, 2018. Polly. Envoy documentation, outlier detection.

blocks.title: In plain words: Decide in advance how long you will wait; then stop waiting.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Decide in advance how long you will wait; then stop waiting.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A call that never returns holds a thread, a connection, and a database cursor forever. A dependency that is slow, not down, is worse than one that is down, because the breaker never sees a failure.
💡 The pattern.
The caller stops waiting after a set time and treats the call as failed.
Timeouts propagate: a caller with 800 milliseconds left should not give its dependency a two-second budget.
Hystrix.

Every Hystrix command has an execution timeout, one second by default, after which the call is abandoned and the fallback runs. The timeout is what turns a slow dependency into a counted failure that can open the circuit.
gRPC deadlines.

gRPC calls carry a deadline rather than a timeout: an absolute point in time, propagated to every downstream call made while serving the request. If the edge gives a request 500 milliseconds, the third service in the chain sees how much of that remains and can refuse work it cannot finish. Google’s 2016 post on deadlines describes the alternative: a chain of services each waiting on the next long after the client has given up.
Envoy.
Envoy applies a route timeout, 15 seconds by default, and a per-try timeout for each retry attempt, so the timeout is configured once in the sidecar and applies to every language.
⚠️ The cost.
Too short, and healthy slow calls fail. Too long, and the timeout protects nothing. The right value is a budget for the whole request, divided among the hops, and few teams write that budget down.
Source: Hystrix wiki, execution.isolation.thread.timeoutInMilliseconds. Sheerin, “gRPC and Deadlines,” 2016. Envoy documentation, route timeouts.

blocks.title: In plain words: Try again a few times, with growing random pauses, and only when it is safe to repeat.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Try again a few times, with growing random pauses, and only when it is safe to repeat.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
Many failures are transient — a dropped connection, a node restarting. Failing the user for a blip is wrong. Retrying a whole fleet at once is worse.
💡 The pattern.
The caller repeats a failed call a limited number of times, only for failures that are safe to repeat, with a growing and randomized delay between attempts.
AWS SDKs.

Marc Brooker’s 2015 post “Exponential Backoff And Jitter” showed with simulation that plain exponential backoff still produces synchronized retry waves, and that “full jitter” — a random delay between zero and the exponential cap — spreads the load and finishes sooner. AWS SDKs implement it, and the post is cited by every retry library since.
Google.

The SRE book’s chapter on overload gives the budgets Google uses: a request is retried at most three times, and a client stops retrying when retries exceed ten percent of its requests, because a retry storm against an overloaded service is a self-inflicted outage. gRPC lets a service publish its retry policy — which status codes are retryable, how many attempts — so every client behaves the same.
Envoy and Stripe.
Envoy retry budgets cap concurrent retries as a percentage of active requests. Stripe’s client libraries retry automatically, and can, because they send the same idempotency key on every attempt.
⚠️ The cost.
Retries multiply load exactly when the dependency can least take it. They are safe only for idempotent operations, which is why the idempotent-consumer chapter exists.

Source: Brooker, “Exponential Backoff And Jitter,” AWS Architecture Blog, 2015. Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 21, “Handling Overload,” 2016. gRPC retry design. Envoy documentation, retry budgets. Stripe API reference.

blocks.title: In plain words: Compartments: one flooding dependency cannot sink the whole ship.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Compartments: one flooding dependency cannot sink the whole ship.
