blocks.alt: Nygard’s metaphor drawn: watertight compartments in a hull. Hystrix thread pools, Shopify’s Semian tickets, and AWS cells are the same idea at three sizes.
blocks.caption: Nygard’s metaphor drawn: watertight compartments in a hull. Hystrix thread pools, Shopify’s Semian tickets, and AWS cells are the same idea at three sizes.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
One slow dependency consumes every thread in the caller’s pool, and calls to healthy dependencies queue behind it. One tenant or one region takes down all of them.
💡 The pattern.
Isolate the resources used for one dependency, one tenant, or one partition, so exhaustion stays inside the compartment.
Nygard took the name from a ship’s hull: a breach floods one section.
Hystrix.

Each Hystrix command group runs on its own thread pool, ten threads by default. If the recommendations service hangs, its ten threads fill and further calls are rejected immediately with the fallback, while the threads for the catalog service are untouched. Semaphore isolation is the lighter alternative for in-process calls.
Shopify Semian.

Semian (2015) is Shopify’s resiliency library for Ruby. Its bulkhead is a ticket count per resource — MySQL, Redis, an HTTP host: only so many worker processes may hold a connection to that resource at once, so a slow shard cannot absorb every worker on the host. Circuit breakers sit beside the bulkheads in the same library.
AWS.

At infrastructure scale the bulkhead is the cell. Peter Vosshall’s 2018 talk on minimizing blast radius describes services partitioned into cells, each a complete copy serving a slice of customers, so a failure is bounded to one cell; availability zones and Route 53’s shuffle sharding are the same idea at other layers.
⚠️ The cost.
Capacity is fragmented: ten pools of ten are less flexible than one pool of a hundred. Pool sizes have to be tuned, and the wrong size is either a bottleneck or no protection.

Source: Nygard, Release It!, 2007. Hystrix wiki, thread pool isolation. Shopify Semian, 2015. Vosshall, “How AWS Minimizes the Blast Radius of Failures,” re:Invent 2018. MacCárthaigh on shuffle sharding, AWS Architecture Blog.
In a monolith the session knows who the user is. In a service system the fourth service in the chain has to know too, without calling back to a session store on every hop.

blocks.alt: Part map — Carrying identity: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.
blocks.caption: Part map — Carrying identity: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: The standard for how a client obtains a token.
JSON Web Token: a signed token a service can verify without a network call.
A statement inside a token, such as the user’s identifier.
Both ends prove their identity with certificates; SPIFFE names workloads.
A service misusing the authority of the token it was handed.

blocks.title: In plain words: The caller’s identity travels with the request, signed, so every service can check it locally.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
The caller’s identity travels with the request, signed, so every service can check it locally.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

The service that handles a request has to know who asked and what they may do. A shared session database puts every service on one store; asking the identity service on every hop puts it on every path.
💡 The pattern.
A token carrying the caller’s identity and claims travels with the request from service to service.
Each service verifies the token’s signature locally and reads the claims. The identity service is called once, when the token is issued.
OAuth 2.0 and JWT.

OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749, 2012) standardized how a client obtains a token; JSON Web Token (RFC 7519, 2015) standardized a signed, self-describing token that a service can verify without a network call. Together they are the identity layer of most public microservice APIs.
Microsoft eShopOnContainers.

The Identity service issues JWTs. Ordering and Basket validate the signature against the issuer’s keys and take the user identifier from a claim. No service holds a session, and no service calls Identity on a request path.
Netflix Passport.

Netflix’s 2021 post on edge authentication describes the problem at scale: devices authenticate in many ways — cookies, device tokens, partner tokens — and every service used to parse them. Zuul now terminates all of them and mints a Passport, a short-lived signed identity token, that travels with the request to every downstream service. Services read one format, and a change in a device’s authentication method is a change in Zuul alone.
SPIFFE.

Service identity is the other half. In Istio, each workload gets an X.509 certificate with a SPIFFE identity and calls are mutually authenticated over TLS; that certificate says which service is calling, while the access token says on whose behalf.
⚠️ The cost.

Tokens expire and have to be refreshed; keys rotate; a leaked long-lived token is a credential. A service that forwards a token it received can act with the caller’s full authority, which is the confused-deputy problem the pattern does not solve by itself.

Source: RFC 6749, 2012; RFC 7519, 2015. Microsoft, eShopOnContainers Identity service. Casella et al., “Edge Authentication and Token-Agnostic Identity Propagation,” Netflix Tech Blog, 2021. SPIFFE and Istio security documentation.

A request is now a path across processes. Seven patterns make that path visible after the fact. Most of the tools in this part were built by the companies in the earlier parts because nothing else existed.

blocks.alt: Part map — Observing the running system: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.
blocks.caption: Part map — Observing the running system: the patterns of this part and the software that shows each one.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: One identifier stamped on every log line of one request.
Numbers recorded against time.
How many distinct label values a metric has; too many and it becomes a log.
One hop’s timing record; the tree of spans for one request.
‘95 percent of requests finished within…’ — a measure that ignores the average.
A store that can be added to but never edited.

blocks.title: In plain words: Ship every service’s logs to one searchable place, tied together by a request ID.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Ship every service’s logs to one searchable place, tied together by a request ID.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A request touched twelve services on twelve hosts. The logs are in twelve files, and the host that wrote one of them has already been replaced.
💡 The pattern.
Every service writes structured logs; an agent ships them to one searchable store; a correlation ID in every line ties the twelve together.
ELK.

Elasticsearch (2010), Logstash (2009), and Kibana (2011) were three separate open-source projects that became one stack because operators kept combining them: Logstash to collect and parse, Elasticsearch to index, Kibana to search. For most of the 2010s “ELK” was the name for the pattern. Splunk (2003) is the commercial version that preceded it.
Fluentd and Loki.

Fluentd (2011, later a CNCF project) and its lighter sibling Fluent Bit became the shipping agents in Kubernetes, running as a DaemonSet on every node and reading container stdout. Grafana Loki (2018) made the opposite indexing choice from Elasticsearch — index only labels, not the text — because at container scale full-text indexing of logs was the largest line item.
⚠️ The cost.
Volume and cost, which is why Loki exists. Aggregation only pays if the logs are structured and carry the correlation ID, and that discipline has to be enforced in the chassis or the template.
Source: Elastic, project histories. Fluentd, CNCF. Grafana Labs, Loki announcement, 2018.

blocks.title: In plain words: Counts and timings over time, so health can be seen at a glance.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Counts and timings over time, so health can be seen at a glance.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
Is the system healthy right now, and was it healthy at 3 a.m.? Logs answer that slowly and expensively. Operators need numbers over time.
💡 The pattern.
Each service records counters, timers, and gauges about its operations — requests, errors, latency percentiles — and a collector stores them as time series for dashboards and alerts.
Etsy.

Ian Malpass’s 2011 post “Measure Anything, Measure Everything” released StatsD, a tiny daemon that takes UDP packets from application code and forwards aggregated metrics to Graphite, the time-series store Orbitz had open-sourced in 2008. The message was cultural: make emitting a metric one line of code so engineers measure everything.
Prometheus.

Built at SoundCloud from 2012 by engineers who had used Google’s Borgmon, released in 2015, and the second project accepted by the CNCF in 2016. Prometheus pulls metrics from an HTTP endpoint on each instance, stores them with labels, and its query language made the “four golden signals” — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — a dashboard convention. It is the default metrics system of Kubernetes.
Netflix Atlas and Uber M3.
Netflix released Atlas (2014) as a dimensional time-series store for its fleet, and Uber released M3 (2018) as a Prometheus-compatible store built for the cardinality of thousands of services.
⚠️ The cost.
Cardinality: a label per user or per request turns a metric into a log. Alert fatigue when every metric has a threshold. The numbers say that something is wrong, not what; tracing says what.

Source: Malpass, “Measure Anything, Measure Everything,” Etsy Code as Craft, 2011. Prometheus project history; CNCF, 2016. Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 6, 2016. Netflix Atlas, 2014. Uber M3, 2018.

blocks.title: In plain words: A permanent record of who did what, when — kept for the regulator.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
A permanent record of who did what, when — kept for the regulator.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
Who changed this setting, deleted this record, or granted this permission, and when? Application logs rotate; a regulator or a security team needs a record that does not.
💡 The pattern.

User and administrative actions are recorded — who, what, when, from where — in a durable, append-only store that is kept for as long as policy requires and cannot be edited by the systems it records.
AWS CloudTrail.

CloudTrail (2013) records every API call made in an AWS account, by which principal, from which address, with what parameters, and delivers the log to S3. It is the record that incident response and compliance in the cloud start from, and a model for what a service’s audit log should contain.
Kubernetes, GitHub, Slack.

The Kubernetes API server writes an audit log, governed by a policy that says which requests to record and at what detail. GitHub’s and Slack’s enterprise audit logs expose the same kind of record — who invited whom, who changed a setting — to customers through an API, because the customers’ own compliance depends on it.
Stripe.
Stripe’s stored event history is a domain-event feed and an audit log at once: every state change is recorded with its time and its cause, and the events are retrievable later.
⚠️ The cost.
Retention and storage, immutability that the application itself cannot bypass, and personal data in the record that privacy law then governs.
Source: AWS CloudTrail, 2013. Kubernetes documentation, auditing. GitHub and Slack audit log APIs. Stripe API reference, Events.

blocks.title: In plain words: Follow one request across every service it touched, hop by hop.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Follow one request across every service it touched, hop by hop.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A request was slow. Which of the nine services it passed through was slow, and was it slow because of the tenth service that one of them called?
💡 The pattern.
The edge assigns each request a trace ID.
Every hop records a span — start, end, service, operation — tagged with that ID and the parent span, and passes the IDs on in headers. A collector assembles the spans into a tree.
Google Dapper.

The 2010 Dapper paper described the system Google had run since 2005: trace and span IDs propagated through Stubby RPCs, sampling to keep overhead negligible, and a central store. Nearly every tracer since is a Dapper implementation.
Twitter Zipkin and Uber Jaeger.

Twitter open-sourced Zipkin in 2012 as Dapper for Finagle. Uber built Jaeger in 2015 when Zipkin did not fit its scale and polyglot services, open-sourced it in 2017, and gave it to the CNCF. OpenTracing (2016) and OpenCensus (2018) then merged into OpenTelemetry (2019) so that instrumentation is written once, and the W3C Trace Context header (2020) fixed the format of the IDs on the wire so any proxy can propagate them.
Netflix Edgar.

Netflix’s 2020 post on Edgar shows the pattern used for support rather than performance: for a given customer’s stream session, Edgar assembles the trace, the logs, and the metadata from every service involved so an engineer can see why one playback failed.
⚠️ The cost.

Every hop has to propagate the headers, including queues and asynchronous work, or the trace breaks. Sampling trades completeness for storage; Netflix chose to keep more because the missing trace is always the one support needs.

Source: Sigelman et al., “Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure,” Google, 2010. Twitter, Zipkin, 2012. Uber Engineering, Jaeger, 2017. OpenTelemetry, 2019. W3C Trace Context, 2020. Netflix Tech Blog, “Edgar: Solving Mysteries Faster with Observability,” 2020.

blocks.title: In plain words: Errors reported to one place that groups them and tells the owner.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Errors reported to one place that groups them and tells the owner.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
An exception was logged somewhere in four hundred services. Nobody read the log line, or a thousand identical lines hid the one that mattered.
💡 The pattern.
Exceptions are reported to a central tracker that groups identical errors, counts occurrences, attaches the release and the request context, and notifies the owning team of new and regressed errors.
Sentry.

Sentry began in 2008 as David Cramer’s Django plugin that stored exceptions in a database instead of a log file, became a standalone open-source server in 2010, and became the default of the category. Its fingerprinting groups an exception by stack trace and message, its release tracking says which deploy introduced an error, and its SDKs attach the user, the request, and the breadcrumbs that led to the failure.
Airbrake, Rollbar, Bugsnag, Crashlytics.

Airbrake (as Hoptoad, 2008) did the same for Rails applications; Rollbar (2012) and Bugsnag (2013) followed for services; Crashlytics (2011) did it for mobile clients and became part of Firebase. Together they made “an exception with no ticket” a thing a team could notice.
⚠️ The cost.
Noise if every handled exception is reported. Stack traces and request bodies carry personal data into a third-party store, which has to be scrubbed.
Source: Sentry project history. Airbrake, Rollbar, Bugsnag, Crashlytics.

blocks.title: In plain words: An endpoint that says ‘alive’, ‘ready’, or ‘not now’.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
An endpoint that says ‘alive’, ‘ready’, or ‘not now’.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The registry, the load balancer, and the orchestrator all need to know whether an instance can take traffic, and a process that is running is not the same as a process that is working.
💡 The pattern.
The service exposes an endpoint that reports its health, and a monitor calls it.
The best versions distinguish “I am alive” from “I am ready to serve” from “my dependencies are reachable.”
Kubernetes.

Kubernetes made the distinction a platform primitive. A liveness probe failing restarts the container. A readiness probe failing removes the pod from the Service’s endpoints without restarting it — the pod is alive, but not to be sent traffic. A startup probe (stable since 1.20) holds the other two off while a slow application boots. The probes are how third-party registration knows what to register.
Spring Boot Actuator and Dropwizard.

Dropwizard (2011) shipped a health-check registry in its first release, and Spring Boot Actuator’s /health endpoint (2014) aggregates indicators for the database, disk, and message broker into one status. Consul and Eureka poll such endpoints; AWS load balancers call one before routing to a target.
⚠️ The cost.

A shallow check says nothing; a deep check that calls every dependency turns a dependency’s outage into the caller being marked unhealthy and removed, which is a cascade. The design of the check is a design of what failure should do.
Source: Kubernetes documentation, liveness, readiness, and startup probes. Dropwizard, 2011. Spring Boot Actuator, 2014. HashiCorp Consul, health checks.

blocks.title: In plain words: Record every change, so an outage can be lined up with what changed just before it.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Record every change, so an outage can be lined up with what changed just before it.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

The error rate went up at 14:07. Something changed at 14:06, and the team spends an hour finding out what. The SRE book’s estimate is that roughly seventy percent of outages follow a change to a live system.
💡 The pattern.
Every deployment and configuration change is recorded — what, who, when, which version — in a place that can be laid over the metrics, so an incident can be lined up with the change that preceded it.
Etsy.

Etsy’s Deployinator (2010) pushed a marker into Graphite on every deploy, and every Etsy graph showed deploys as vertical lines. An engineer looking at a latency graph saw the line and the jump together. Erik Kastner’s “Quantum of Deployment” made the deploy line a convention, and Grafana annotations are its descendant.
Netflix Spinnaker and Kubernetes.

Spinnaker (2015) keeps the execution history of every pipeline: which image, which cluster, who triggered it, and what happened. Kubernetes records a Deployment’s revision history, and kubectl rollout history with a change-cause annotation gives the operator the list of what changed, and rollout undo to reverse it.
⚠️ The cost.
Only code deploys get recorded unless the team also records feature-flag flips, configuration pushes, and infrastructure changes, and those are the changes that are hardest to see.

Source: Kastner, “Quantum of Deployment,” Etsy Code as Craft, 2010. Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering, 2016, on the share of outages caused by change. Netflix Spinnaker, 2015. Kubernetes documentation, Deployments.

The unit that starts, stops, and scales has changed three times in twenty years: from many processes on a server, to one image per virtual machine, to one container per pod, and to the function. The pattern language keeps all of them.

items.definition: Linux kernel features that isolate a process’s resources and view of the system — the substance of a container.
The packaged, immutable artifact a container or VM starts from.
A set of identical VMs kept at a target count.
Launch the new fleet, switch traffic, terminate the old.
The delay before an idle serverless function can answer.
Running no instances at all while idle.

blocks.text: Chapter 45. Multiple service instances per host

blocks.title: In plain words: Several services share one machine. Cheap, and they trip over each other.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Several services share one machine. Cheap, and they trip over each other.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
Machines are expensive and mostly idle. Several services on one machine use it better.
💡 The pattern.
Several service instances share one host and one operating system, as separate processes or as modules inside one process.
This was the default before virtualization made machines cheap to create.
Application servers.

WebLogic, WebSphere, JBoss, and Tomcat were built for this: one JVM hosting many deployed applications, each a WAR or EAR file, sharing the heap, the thread pools, and the process lifecycle. Microsoft’s IIS hosted many sites and application pools on one server in the same way. Most of the services extracted from monoliths in 2010–2014 first ran like this, several to a host, managed by the operations team’s scripts.
Why it ended.

One application’s memory leak took down its neighbors; two applications needed different library versions; nobody could say which service used the CPU. The container pattern below is this pattern with the isolation added back.
⚠️ The cost.
No isolation of resources or failures. Dependency conflicts. Per-service resource use is invisible. Deploying one service risks the others in the process.
Source: Richardson, microservices.io, “Multiple service instances per host.” Vendor documentation for the application servers named.

blocks.title: In plain words: One service per machine. Isolated, and wasteful.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
One service per machine. Isolated, and wasteful.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
Isolation. A service that has a machine to itself cannot be starved or crashed by a neighbor, and its resource use is the machine’s.
💡 The pattern.
Each service instance runs on its own host, physical or virtual.
The next two chapters are the virtual and container forms; this one is the general case and its physical origin.
Google.

Barroso, Dean, and Hölzle’s 2003 paper on Google’s search cluster describes machines dedicated by role: index servers, document servers, and web servers, each machine running one role, with thousands of cheap commodity machines instead of a few large ones. One role per host is how Google reasoned about capacity before Borg packed roles onto shared machines inside containers.
Stack Overflow.

Craver’s 2016 inventory is one role per physical server: web servers, SQL Server, Redis, the tag engine, Elasticsearch, HAProxy, each on its own dedicated hardware. It is the pattern applied to a monolith’s tiers rather than to microservices, and it shows the pattern is about isolation, not about service count.
⚠️ The cost.
Utilization is low and provisioning is slow when the host is physical. The virtual machine fixed the second problem and the container fixed the first.
Source: Barroso, Dean, and Hölzle, “Web Search for a Planet: The Google Cluster Architecture,” IEEE Micro, 2003. Craver, 2016.

blocks.text: Chapter 47. Service instance per virtual machine

blocks.title: In plain words: Bake the service into a machine image; deploy by launching copies; never patch, replace.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Bake the service into a machine image; deploy by launching copies; never patch, replace.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The team wants one service per host, provisioned in minutes, replaced rather than patched, and scaled by count.
💡 The pattern.
Each service is packaged as a virtual machine image.
Deploying means launching instances of the image; scaling means launching more; a new version is a new image, and old instances are terminated rather than updated.
Netflix.

From 2011 Netflix baked every service into its own Amazon Machine Image — “Building with Legos,” as the 2011 post called it — with a tool later open-sourced as Aminator, and launched it into an Auto Scaling group with Asgard (2012). A deploy was a red/black switch: launch the new group, move traffic, terminate the old. Nothing was ever changed on a running instance; the image was the release. Spinnaker (2015) generalized the pipeline across clouds.
HashiCorp Packer.
Packer (2013) made image baking a general tool: one template builds the same image for AWS, VMware, and later Docker, and the immutable-server practice spread beyond Netflix.
⚠️ The cost.
Minutes to boot, gigabytes per image, and a whole operating system per service. The container kept the immutability and removed most of the weight.
Source: Ciancutti, “Building with Legos,” Netflix Tech Blog, 2011. Netflix Asgard, 2012; Aminator, 2013. HashiCorp Packer, 2013. Netflix Spinnaker, 2015.

blocks.title: In plain words: The isolation of a virtual machine at a fraction of the weight; an orchestrator places them.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
The isolation of a virtual machine at a fraction of the weight; an orchestrator places them.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
One service per virtual machine is isolated but heavy. Teams want the isolation and the immutable image without a kernel per service.
💡 The pattern.
Each service instance runs in its own container: an image with the service and its dependencies, isolated by kernel namespaces and cgroups, sharing the host kernel.
An orchestrator schedules containers onto hosts.
Google Borg.

Google had run every task in a cgroups-based container on shared machines for a decade before the 2015 Borg paper described it; Google contributed cgroups to Linux in 2006–2007 for this. Kubernetes (2014, 1.0 in 2015) is Borg’s lessons rewritten for everyone else.
Docker.

Docker (2013) made the container image portable and the developer experience simple, and it is the reason the pattern is called container rather than cgroup. eShopOnContainers is named for it: one Dockerfile per service, composed for local development with docker-compose and deployed to Kubernetes.
Netflix Titus, Spotify Helios, Airbnb, Monzo.

Netflix built Titus (in production from about 2015, open-sourced 2018) to run containers on its existing VM fleet and scheduling. Spotify open-sourced Helios (2014) to run Docker before Kubernetes existed. Airbnb moved its services to Kubernetes in 2018 and Monzo has run on it since 2016.
⚠️ The cost.
An image supply chain to secure and an orchestrator to operate. The isolation is weaker than a VM’s, which matters for multi-tenant platforms.

Source: Verma et al., “Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg,” EuroSys 2015. Docker, 2013. Kubernetes, 2014–2015. Netflix Titus, 2018. Spotify Helios, 2014. Cebula, Airbnb, KubeCon 2018. Monzo engineering talks.

blocks.title: In plain words: Upload code; the platform runs it on demand and bills per run.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Upload code; the platform runs it on demand and bills per run.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The team wants to deploy code, not instances. Idle capacity should cost nothing; a burst should be absorbed without a scaling policy.
💡 The pattern.
The platform runs the service’s code on demand in response to an event or a request, scales the number of running copies itself, including to zero, and bills per invocation.
The team manages no host, virtual machine, or container.
AWS Lambda.

Lambda (announced 2014) defined the category: upload a function, connect it to an event source — an S3 upload, a queue message, an HTTP request through API Gateway — and the platform runs it. Netflix was an early public case, using Lambda for encoding triggers, backup validation, and security checks that fired on events rather than running as services. Google Cloud Functions and Azure Functions followed in 2016; Cloudflare Workers (2017) ran functions at the edge; Knative (2018) brought scale-to-zero to Kubernetes.
Amazon Prime Video.

The 2023 monitoring-service case is the boundary of the pattern. A high-throughput pipeline built from Step Functions and Lambda, passing video frames through S3 between steps, cost more in orchestration and storage transfers than the compute; moved into one long-running ECS process, it cost about a tenth. Serverless suits event-driven and bursty work; it suits a steady stream less well.
⚠️ The cost.
Cold starts, execution time limits, and a vendor’s event model. At high steady throughput, per-invocation billing exceeds a reserved instance, which is what Prime Video measured.
Source: AWS Lambda, 2014. Netflix presentations at re:Invent, 2014–2015. Kolny, Prime Video Tech, 2023. Cloudflare Workers, 2017. Knative, 2018. Richardson, microservices.io, “Serverless deployment.”

blocks.title: In plain words: Say ‘run three copies behind this name’; the platform makes it so.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Say ‘run three copies behind this name’; the platform makes it so.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A team should be able to say “run three copies of this behind this name” and have it happen, without owning the machines, the placement, the restarts, or the load balancer configuration.
💡 The pattern.

An automated platform takes a packaged service and provides deployment, scaling, placement, health management, and a service abstraction — a stable name that routes to whatever instances currently exist.
Heroku, App Engine, Cloud Foundry.

Heroku (2007) made the platform a git push: the buildpack builds the application, dynos run it, the router gives it a name. Google App Engine (2008) offered the same shape with Google’s runtimes. Cloud Foundry (2011) was the open-source platform enterprises ran themselves. Each one is the platform-as-a-service chapter of this series applied to one service.
Kubernetes.

Kubernetes is the platform most microservice systems now sit on. A Deployment declares the image and replica count and performs rolling updates; the scheduler places pods; the kubelet restarts them; a Service gives them a name. The platform owns everything the deployment patterns above used to leave to scripts.
Netflix Spinnaker and Titus.

Netflix built its platform in two parts: Spinnaker (2015) for the delivery pipeline — bake, deploy, canary analysis, red/black — and Titus for container scheduling. Together they are a service deployment platform assembled by one company for one fleet, which is what most large companies did before Kubernetes made it a commodity.
⚠️ The cost.
A platform team, and abstractions that leak when a service needs something the platform did not foresee: a GPU, a privileged port, a stateful volume.

Source: Heroku, 2007. Google App Engine, 2008. Cloud Foundry, 2011. Kubernetes documentation, Deployments and Services. Netflix Spinnaker, 2015; Titus, 2018. The PaaS and Kubernetes chapters of this series.

Every service needs logging, configuration, discovery, retries, and metrics. The question is whether those live in a library every service compiles in, or in a process beside the service. The industry answered library first, then proxy.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: A need every service shares: logging, configuration, discovery, retries.
A setting that can change at runtime without a restart.
A credential issued for a time and revoked afterwards.
The paved, expected way to build and run a service.
What configures the proxies; the proxies that carry traffic.

blocks.title: In plain words: A shared framework, so the fortieth service does not rebuild logging and health checks.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
A shared framework, so the fortieth service does not rebuild logging and health checks.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The fortieth service should not reimplement health checks, metrics, configuration loading, and the discovery client. Forty copies of that code will be forty slightly different copies.
💡 The pattern.
A framework handles the cross-cutting concerns and leaves the team to write domain logic.
Starting a service means depending on the chassis and adding handlers.
Dropwizard.

Coda Hale released Dropwizard at Yammer in 2011: Jetty, Jersey, Jackson, Metrics, and health checks assembled into one opinionated bundle so that a production-ready HTTP service was a main method and a resource class. It was the first widely used chassis, and Metrics — its instrumentation library — outlived it.
Spring Boot and Spring Cloud Netflix.

Spring Boot (2014) made the Java service a self-contained jar with an embedded server and auto-configuration. Spring Cloud Netflix (2015) wrapped Eureka, Ribbon, Hystrix, and Archaius as starters, so a Spring Boot application registered, discovered, and broke circuits by adding dependencies. For several years this pair was the default chassis of enterprise microservices.
Twitter Finagle, Monzo Typhon.

Finagle is a chassis for RPC: tracing, load balancing, retries, and metrics are filters composed around every server and client. Monzo’s Go services share Typhon, an RPC library with common middleware, so that every one of its 1,500 services speaks and observes the same way.
⚠️ The cost.

Language lock-in: the chassis exists for one runtime, and a company with four languages needs four. Upgrading the chassis across hundreds of services is a project of its own, which is the reason the sidecar and the mesh appeared.
Source: Hale, Dropwizard, 2011. Spring Boot 1.0, 2014. Spring Cloud Netflix, 2015. Twitter Finagle. Monzo Typhon. Richardson, microservices.io, “Microservice chassis.”

blocks.title: In plain words: Settings and secrets live outside the build, so one image runs everywhere.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Settings and secrets live outside the build, so one image runs everywhere.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The same image must run in test, staging, and production with different database addresses, credentials, and limits, and a configuration change should not require a build.
💡 The pattern.
Configuration lives outside the service package — environment variables, a configuration service, mounted files — and is read at startup or refreshed at runtime.
Secrets are configuration with stricter handling.
Twelve-Factor App.

Adam Wiggins’s 2011 manifesto from Heroku made it a rule: factor III, store config in the environment, because config varies between deploys and code does not. The test it proposes is whether the codebase could be open-sourced without leaking a credential.
Netflix Archaius and Spring Cloud Config.

Archaius (2012) gave Netflix services dynamic properties: values polled from a source and changed at runtime without restart, which is how Hystrix thresholds were tuned during incidents. Spring Cloud Config (2015) served configuration from a Git repository so that a configuration change was a commit with history.
Kubernetes and Vault.

Kubernetes made ConfigMaps and Secrets first-class objects mounted into pods as files or environment variables, separating the image from its settings by construction. HashiCorp Vault (2015) added secrets that are issued dynamically, leased, and revoked, so a database credential is minted for one service instance and expires with it.
⚠️ The cost.

Configuration drift between environments, and a configuration change that is not versioned and reviewed is a production change nobody can trace. Secrets in environment variables leak into logs and process lists.
Source: Wiggins, The Twelve-Factor App, 2011. Netflix Archaius, 2012. Spring Cloud Config, 2015. Kubernetes documentation, ConfigMaps and Secrets. HashiCorp Vault, 2015.

blocks.title: In plain words: A ready-made starter service to copy: build, pipeline, and metrics already wired.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
A ready-made starter service to copy: build, pipeline, and metrics already wired.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A new service takes a day to set up — build, CI, Dockerfile, metrics, health endpoint, ownership metadata — and each team sets it up differently.
💡 The pattern.
A copyable starter service already contains the build, the chassis, and the standard cross-cutting concerns.
A new service is generated from it and the team fills in the domain.
Spotify Backstage.

Backstage (open-sourced 2020, later a CNCF project) is Spotify’s developer portal, and its Software Templates are the pattern as a product: a template scaffolds a repository with the CI pipeline, the Dockerfile, the observability hooks, and the catalog entry that records who owns it. Spotify calls the result a “golden path” — the paved road that a team is expected to take unless it has a reason not to.
Spring Initializr and dotnet new.

start.spring.io generates a Spring Boot project with the chosen starters wired; dotnet new generates a .NET web API with the standard layout. Both are service templates without the company-specific parts, which each company then adds.
Monzo.

Monzo’s engineers describe generating a new service from a standard skeleton so that the shared libraries, the RPC layer, and the metrics are present before any domain code is written; that is how a small company came to have 1,500 services that look alike.
⚠️ The cost.

A template is copied, not linked. When the template improves, the services generated from it last year do not, which is the argument for putting as much as possible in the chassis and as little as possible in the template.
Source: Spotify Backstage, 2020, Software Templates. Spring Initializr. .NET SDK templates. Monzo engineering blog and talks, 2018–2019.

blocks.title: In plain words: A helper process riding beside the service, handling the plumbing in any language.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
A helper process riding beside the service, handling the plumbing in any language.

blocks.alt: A motorcycle with a sidecar. Prana rode beside non-JVM services at Netflix; Envoy rides beside every pod under Istio. Photo: Infrogmation, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
blocks.caption: A motorcycle with a sidecar. Prana rode beside non-JVM services at Netflix; Envoy rides beside every pod under Istio. Photo: Infrogmation, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The chassis solved cross-cutting concerns for one language. The Python service and the Node service are still on their own, and upgrading the chassis still means redeploying every service.
💡 The pattern.
The cross-cutting concerns run in a separate process or container beside the service instance, sharing its host or pod, and handle traffic, configuration, or logs on its behalf.
The service stays language-agnostic and small.
Netflix Prana.

Prana (2014) is the earliest well-known sidecar: a Java process deployed beside a non-JVM service that registers it with Eureka, gives it Ribbon-style client-side load balancing, and serves Archaius configuration over a local HTTP port. The Python service got the Netflix stack without a line of Java.
Lyft Envoy and Istio.

Envoy (open-sourced 2016) is a proxy written to be a sidecar: it handles every inbound and outbound connection for the service next to it, adding TLS, retries, timeouts, breakers, and tracing headers. Istio (2017) injects an Envoy container into every pod automatically, so the service developer does not know it is there. Brendan Burns and David Oppenheimer’s 2016 paper named sidecar, ambassador, and adapter as the container patterns; the Kubernetes pod — containers sharing a network namespace — is what made the sidecar cheap to deploy, and Kubernetes 1.28 (2023) added native sidecar containers with their own lifecycle.
Dapr.

Microsoft’s Dapr (2019) puts service invocation, pub/sub, and state stores behind a sidecar’s local HTTP and gRPC API, so the application calls localhost and the sidecar talks to Redis, Kafka, or Service Bus.
⚠️ The cost.
A second process per instance — memory and CPU multiplied by the number of pods — and a latency hop on every call. In exchange, upgrading the sidecar fleet is one rollout instead of hundreds.

Source: Netflix Tech Blog, Prana, 2014. Klein, Envoy, Lyft, 2016. Istio, 2017. Burns and Oppenheimer, “Design patterns for container-based distributed systems,” HotCloud 2016. Kubernetes 1.28 release notes. Dapr, 2019.

blocks.title: In plain words: Sidecars everywhere, plus a control tower that configures them all.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Sidecars everywhere, plus a control tower that configures them all.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

A sidecar beside every service still needs to be told where services are, what the retry policy is, and which certificates to use. Configuring a thousand sidecars by hand is the chassis problem again.
💡 The pattern.

A data plane of sidecar proxies mediates all service-to-service communication, and a control plane configures them: discovery, load balancing, mutual TLS, retries, timeouts, breakers, and telemetry, applied by policy rather than by code in each service.
Linkerd.

Buoyant, founded by former Twitter engineers, released Linkerd in February 2016, built on Finagle; William Morgan gave the category its name. Linkerd 2 (2018) rewrote the data plane as a small Rust proxy for Kubernetes.
Istio and Envoy.

Istio (May 2017, from Google, IBM, and Lyft) paired Envoy as the data plane with a control plane that distributes routing, security, and telemetry policy to every sidecar. It brought the discovery, breaker, retry, and tracing patterns of the earlier parts out of the Netflix libraries and into the platform. Consul Connect (2018) and AWS App Mesh (2018) followed with the same shape.
Monzo and Airbnb.

Monzo ran Linkerd early and later moved its data plane to Envoy, and its 2019 network-isolation work — policy for which of 1,500 services may call which — is the kind of rule a mesh exists to enforce. Airbnb’s SmartStack (2013), with a registrar and a per-host HAProxy on every machine, was a service mesh before the term, missing only the central control plane.
⚠️ The cost.

A control plane to operate and understand, a proxy hop per call, and a category of failures — sidecar injection, certificate rotation, policy misconfiguration — that did not exist before. The mesh moves the reliability patterns; it does not touch the data patterns. A saga is still a saga.

Source: Buoyant, Linkerd, 2016; Morgan, “What’s a service mesh? And why do I need one?,” 2017. Istio, 2017. Klein, Envoy, 2016. HashiCorp Consul Connect, 2018. Kleeman, Monzo, 2019; Monzo engineering talks. Serebryany, Airbnb, 2013.

blocks.title: In plain words: A sidecar for outbound calls only: the app talks to localhost; the ambassador finds and secures the destination.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
A sidecar for outbound calls only: the app talks to localhost; the ambassador finds and secures the destination.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A service makes outbound calls that need connectivity logic — discovery, TLS, retries, connection pooling — and the team wants that logic out of the application and the same across languages.
💡 The pattern.
An outbound proxy beside the service handles connections the service makes.
The service connects to localhost; the ambassador finds the destination, secures the connection, and applies retry and monitoring. It is the sidecar pattern restricted to outbound traffic.
Kubernetes and Cloud SQL Auth Proxy.

Burns and Oppenheimer’s 2016 paper uses an ambassador container for exactly this: the application talks to localhost and the ambassador handles sharding or discovery. Google’s Cloud SQL Auth Proxy is the production case — a sidecar that opens an authenticated, encrypted connection to a Cloud SQL instance and exposes it on a local port, so the application sees a plain database on localhost and never handles certificates.
Airbnb Synapse and Envoy.

Airbnb’s Synapse (2013) configured a local HAProxy with one port per dependency; a service connecting to localhost:3000 reached whichever healthy instances of the dependency existed. Envoy in egress mode does the same for HTTP and gRPC calls leaving a pod.
A naming collision.
Datawire’s Ambassador (2017) is an Envoy-based API gateway for Kubernetes ingress, an edge component, not this pattern. The name is shared; the job is not.
⚠️ The cost.
A hop and a process per instance, as with any sidecar. The name is ambiguous enough that a design document should say which one it means.
Source: Burns and Oppenheimer, HotCloud 2016. Google Cloud SQL Auth Proxy documentation. Serebryany, Airbnb, 2013. Envoy documentation. Azure Architecture Center, “Ambassador pattern.”
A monolith is tested by running it. Four hundred services cannot be stood up on a laptop, and the interesting bugs are between them. Three patterns test a service without the rest.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: A written, executable statement of what a consumer expects from a provider.
A stand-in for a real dependency in a test.
Where contracts and verification results are stored; answers ‘can I deploy?’.
Sealed: a test that needs no shared environment.

blocks.title: In plain words: Callers write down what they depend on; the provider’s build checks it before release.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Callers write down what they depend on; the provider’s build checks it before release.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

The Orders team changes a field name. The three services that call Orders break in production, because nobody knew they depended on that field, and an end-to-end test environment that would have caught it takes a day to stand up and is always broken.
💡 The pattern.
Each consumer writes down the interactions it depends on — this request, this response shape — as an executable contract.
The provider runs every consumer’s contracts in its own build. A provider change that breaks a consumer fails the provider’s build, before deployment. Ian Robinson named the idea in 2006.
Pact.

Pact was written in 2013 by engineers at DiUS working with REA Group, the Australian property site, whose Ruby services kept breaking each other. The consumer’s test runs against a mock provider and records a pact file; the provider’s build replays the pact against the real provider. The Pact Broker stores pacts and verification results, and its can-i-deploy check answers whether this version of a service is compatible with everything currently deployed. Atlassian adopted Pact across its Jira and Bitbucket teams and spoke about it publicly, which is how it reached the enterprise.
Spring Cloud Contract.

Marcin Grzejszczak’s Spring Cloud Contract (2016) puts the contract on the provider side in Groovy or YAML, generates the provider’s tests from it, and publishes WireMock stubs that consumers test against — the same guarantee, with the artifact flowing the other way.
⚠️ The cost.
Contracts to maintain as the API evolves, and a broker to run. The pattern fits known internal consumers; a public API with unknown consumers cannot collect their contracts.
Source: Robinson, “Consumer-Driven Contracts: A Service Evolution Pattern,” 2006. Pact, 2013; Pact Broker. Atlassian talks on Pact adoption, 2017–2018. Spring Cloud Contract, 2016.

blocks.title: In plain words: The caller tests its own client against a stand-in built from the agreed contract.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
The caller tests its own client against a stand-in built from the agreed contract.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The consumer’s client code — the class that calls Orders and parses the reply — has to be tested, and the real Orders service is not available in the consumer’s unit test.
💡 The pattern.
The consumer tests its client against a stub of the provider that is derived from the contract, so the test proves the client can speak the agreed protocol without the provider running.
Pact.

The consumer half of a Pact test is a consumer-side contract test: the client is exercised against Pact’s mock provider, which is configured with the expected interactions and fails the test if the client sends anything else. The pact file that results is the contract the provider will later verify.
Spring Cloud Contract and WireMock.

Spring Cloud Contract publishes WireMock stubs built from the provider’s contracts as a versioned artifact; the consumer’s tests start the stub runner and call it as if it were the provider. WireMock (2011) on its own is the general tool — a programmable HTTP stub — and is what most consumer-side tests use when there is no contract framework.
⚠️ The cost.

A stub that is not derived from the provider’s verified contract drifts, and the consumer passes tests against a provider that no longer exists. The pattern is only as good as the link to the provider’s verification.
Source: Pact documentation, consumer tests. Spring Cloud Contract, stub runner. WireMock, 2011.

blocks.title: In plain words: Test one whole service alone, with a real database and fake neighbors.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
Test one whole service alone, with a real database and fake neighbors.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.

Unit tests pass and the service fails on start because the real database rejects the schema, or because the message serialization differs from what the broker delivers. The team wants to test the whole service, alone.
💡 The pattern.
The service is run as a black box with its real infrastructure dependencies — database, broker — as throwaway instances, and the other services it calls replaced by test doubles.
Tests drive its API and observe its outputs.
Testcontainers.

Richard North’s Testcontainers (2015) starts a real Postgres, Kafka, or Redis in Docker for the duration of a test and tears it down after. It replaced the in-memory database that behaved differently from production, and it is now the standard way a JVM, .NET, Go, or Node service is component-tested.
WireMock and Toxiproxy.

WireMock stands in for the services the component calls. Shopify’s Toxiproxy (2014) sits between the component and its dependencies as a TCP proxy and injects latency, dropped connections, and bandwidth limits on command, so the test can ask what the service does when Redis is slow, not only when it is absent.
Google.

Google’s testing blog described “hermetic servers” in 2012: a server under test started with all its dependencies faked or local, so the test is repeatable and needs no shared environment. eShopOnContainers does the small version with ASP.NET Core’s TestServer hosting a service in-process with test doubles.
⚠️ The cost.
Slower and heavier than unit tests, and the doubles can drift from the real services unless contract tests keep them honest — which is why the three testing patterns are used together.
Source: North, Testcontainers, 2015. WireMock, 2011. Shopify Toxiproxy, 2014. Google Testing Blog, “Hermetic Servers,” 2012. Microsoft, eShopOnContainers functional tests.

blocks.text: Part 15. Composing a screen from many services

runs.t: The page shows the product, its price, the reviews, and the recommendations, and four teams own those. Two patterns decide which tier puts the page together.

blocks.title: Words to know

items.definition: A piece of a page produced by one team’s service.
Edge Side Includes: assembling a page from fragments in a cache or CDN.
A browser element that embeds one page inside another.
Letting one built application load code from another at runtime.
The thin host application that loads the fragments.

blocks.title: In plain words: The server stitches a page from fragments each team produced.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
The server stitches a page from fragments each team produced.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
A page needs HTML from several services, and it should render as one page, quickly, with each fragment owned by the team that owns the data.
💡 The pattern.
The server assembles the page from HTML fragments, each generated by the service that owns that part of the business.
A layout service or template names the fragments; a composer fetches them and streams the page.
Facebook BigPipe.

Changhao Jiang’s 2010 post described BigPipe: a page is split into “pagelets” — the news feed, the chat list, the ads — each generated by its own server-side path, and the page is flushed to the browser in chunks as each pagelet is ready, so the first pagelet renders while the slowest is still being built.
Zalando Mosaic and Tailor.

Zalando’s Mosaic (2016) is BigPipe for a company of many teams: Tailor is a Node service that takes a template naming fragments, fetches each fragment from the team’s service over HTTP, and streams the assembled page; Skipper routes requests to the right template. Each team deploys its fragment service on its own schedule.
Amazon and ESI.

Amazon’s product page is composed on the server from more than a hundred services’ output. Edge Side Includes (2001, from Akamai and Oracle) did the composition in the cache: a page with <esi:include> tags is assembled by Varnish or a CDN from fragments with different cache lifetimes, so the price fragment can be fresh while the description is cached for a day.
⚠️ The cost.
The page is as slow as its slowest fragment unless it streams. Fragments from different teams have to share styling and layout without sharing a codebase, and someone owns the template.
Source: Jiang, “BigPipe: Pipelining web pages for high performance,” Facebook Engineering, 2010. Zalando Tech, Mosaic and Tailor, 2016. Vogels, 2006. W3C Note, Edge Side Includes, 2001.

blocks.title: In plain words: The browser assembles the screen from pieces each team ships independently.

paragraphs.t: In plain words:
The browser assembles the screen from pieces each team ships independently.

runs.t: ❓ The problem.
The application is a single-page app, and one frontend codebase owned by every team has become the frontend monolith: one build, one release, one framework version for everyone.
💡 The pattern.
The client assembles the screen from UI fragments, each built and deployed by the team that owns the business capability behind it.
A shell loads the fragments at runtime; each fragment talks to its own backend.
Spotify.

Spotify’s desktop client of the early 2010s was built from independent web views, each hosted in its own iframe and shipped by its own squad, communicating through a shared bridge. It was the client-side version of the squad structure: a team owned a screen and could release it without a client release.
Micro-frontends.

ThoughtWorks put “micro frontends” on its Technology Radar in 2016 and Cam Jackson’s 2019 article on martinfowler.com described the practice with IKEA, whose web presence was composed from fragments owned by different teams, among the cases. single-spa (2015) is a shell framework that mounts and unmounts independently built applications by route; webpack 5’s Module Federation (2020) lets one build load code from another build at runtime, which removed the iframe.
⚠️ The cost.

Duplicate framework code in the browser unless dependencies are shared carefully, shared state and navigation that no single fragment owns, and a design system to keep ten teams’ fragments looking like one product.

Source: Spotify engineering talks on the desktop client architecture, 2012–2014. ThoughtWorks Technology Radar, November 2016. Jackson, “Micro Frontends,” martinfowler.com, 2019. single-spa, 2015. webpack 5 Module Federation, 2020.

blocks.text: What this fixes for the AI chapter

runs.t: Each chapter now has a named case: the software in which the pattern became ordinary, and the reason that company gave. A later claim that AI has changed a pattern can be tested against that case. Did a generated service include an outbox, or a controller that publishes after commit and hopes? Did a suggested boundary follow a capability, a subdomain, or a table? Did a generated saga choose choreography or orchestration, and did it write the compensations? Did the reliability patterns land in the code, in a chassis, or in a sidecar the tool did not know was there?
The examples in these chapters are the standard the answers will be held to.
Three observations from the chapters travel forward.
First, the data patterns — saga, outbox, replica, CQRS — were designed by hand in every case here, with the business rule and the compensation written by someone who knew the domain.
Second, the reliability and discovery patterns have already moved once, from Netflix’s libraries into Envoy and the mesh, so “where does the pattern live” is a question with precedent.
Third, several companies moved back — Segment, Prime Video, Shopify’s choice never to leave — and each gave a cost as the reason.
Any account of AI’s influence has to say which of these three it touched.

Sources are given at the end of each chapter. The pattern names and groupings follow Chris Richardson, microservices.io and Microservices Patterns (2018), with the companions noted in Answer 4. Lewis and Fowler, “Microservices,” 2014, for the characteristics. Nygard, Release It!, 2007, for the stability patterns. Evans, Domain-Driven Design, 2003, for the subdomain and anti-corruption layer.

blocks.title: Read it again: three things to carry away

paragraphs.t: Each pattern has a named case and a documented cost.
Data patterns were hand-designed everywhere; reliability patterns have already moved once — from libraries into the mesh.
Several companies moved back — Segment, Prime Video, Shopify never left — and each gave a cost as the reason.
